|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a hybrid recommender that combines collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, and business rules to overcome each individual approach's weaknesses.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | A hybrid recommender combines multiple approaches to cover each one's individual weak spots: collaborative filtering (or matrix factorization) provides strong recommendations once enough interaction data exists but fails on cold-start items/users, content-based filtering handles the new-item cold-start case using item attributes alone, and business rules (excluding out-of-stock items, boosting currently promoted items, enforcing diversity so recommendations aren't all near-duplicates of each other) handle practical constraints neither statistical approach captures on its own. A common hybrid architecture blends scores from several underlying models (e.g. weighting a collaborative-filtering score and a content-based score together, with the weighting possibly adjusted based on how much interaction history exists for that specific user or item), or runs content-based filtering specifically as a fallback only for new users/items where collaborative signal doesn't yet exist, switching to collaborative/matrix-factorization recommendations once sufficient history accumulates. |
| **Worked example**      | An e-commerce hybrid recommender might use matrix-factorization-based recommendations for an established customer with months of purchase history, but fall back entirely to content-based recommendations (based on items viewed in the current session alone) for a brand-new visitor with no account history at all, switching approaches based on how much data exists for that specific user.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a well-designed hybrid recommender often weight content-based filtering more heavily for a brand-new user specifically, even if collaborative filtering performs better overall for established users?

\(A\) Content-based filtering always outperforms collaborative filtering regardless of how much user history exists

**(B) A new user has no interaction history for collaborative filtering to use yet, so content-based filtering (which only needs item attributes) is the only approach with enough information to work immediately**

\(C\) Hybrid recommenders never adjust their approach based on how much user history is available

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design (on paper, no need to fully implement) a hybrid recommender strategy for a business scenario of your choice, specifying which signal (collaborative, content-based, or a business rule) you'd use for an established user versus a brand-new user, and why.

**Lecture 254 Evaluating recommender systems**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Time Series + Recommendation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Select and apply appropriate offline evaluation metrics (precision@k, recall@k, NDCG) for a ranked recommendation list, recognising why standard classification metrics don't directly apply.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Evaluating a recommender is different from evaluating a classifier, because the output is a ranked list of a fixed length (k) rather than a single prediction, so standard accuracy doesn't directly apply. Precision@k measures what fraction of the top-k recommended items the user actually engaged with, while recall@k measures what fraction of all items the user actually engaged with appeared somewhere in the top-k list; both ignore the order within that top-k list, which is why NDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) exists -- it rewards a relevant item appearing higher in the ranked list more than the same relevant item appearing lower, directly measuring whether the recommender put its best guesses first, not just whether they appeared somewhere in the list at all. Offline metrics computed against historical interaction data are a useful first-pass filter before a more expensive and realistic online A/B test, but they have a known weakness: they can only evaluate against items a user already interacted with historically, systematically underrating a genuinely novel, good recommendation the user never had the chance to interact with in the historical data at all. |
| **Worked example**      | Two recommenders both achieve identical precision@10 by correctly recommending the same 3 relevant items somewhere within their top 10, but one places those 3 items at ranks 1, 2, 3 while the other places them at ranks 8, 9, 10; NDCG would correctly score the first recommender higher since it ranked the relevant items closer to the top.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why might two recommenders with identical precision@10 scores still receive very different NDCG scores?

\(A\) Precision@10 and NDCG are mathematically guaranteed to always produce identical scores for the same ranked list

**(B) NDCG additionally rewards relevant items appearing higher in the ranked list, which precision@10 ignores since it only counts whether an item appears anywhere in the top 10**

\(C\) NDCG can only be computed for exactly 10 recommended items, unlike precision@k

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Compute precision@5 and NDCG@5 for the recommendations generated by one of your models from Lecture 250, 251 or 252, using a held-out set of items the hypothetical user actually interacted with, and compare the two scores.

**Lecture 255 Building the demand forecasting project**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Time Series + Recommendation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Assemble a complete demand forecasting project combining time series decomposition, a properly walk-forward-validated model, and engineered time features.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Project lecture: select a demand-style dataset (retail sales, website traffic, or similar), perform and document a trend/seasonality decomposition (Lecture 241), choose and justify a forecasting approach (ARIMA, exponential smoothing, Prophet, or a feature-engineered tabular regression model, Lectures 243-247) based on the series' actual structure, evaluate it using proper walk-forward validation (Lecture 245) with both RMSE and MAPE (Lecture 248), and produce a short write-up justifying the model choice and reporting honest, leakage-free performance -- the capstone deliverable for this month's project before the extra-practice depth lectures. |
| **Worked example**      | A retail demand forecasting project decomposes 2 years of weekly sales data, identifies strong yearly seasonality, selects Holt-Winters exponential smoothing as the best-justified match for that structure, evaluates it with 4-fold walk-forward validation, and reports both RMSE (for internal technical review) and MAPE (for a one-paragraph business-facing summary).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why must this project's final reported accuracy figures come specifically from walk-forward validation rather than any other evaluation approach covered earlier this program?

\(A\) Walk-forward validation is simply a formality with no effect on whether the reported numbers are trustworthy

**(B) Any other splitting approach risks leaking future information into model training, which would make the project's reported forecasting accuracy dishonest and unrepresentative of real deployment performance**

\(C\) Walk-forward validation always produces higher accuracy numbers than other validation approaches, which is the only reason to prefer it

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Complete your demand forecasting project: perform a decomposition, select and justify a forecasting approach, evaluate it with walk-forward validation reporting both RMSE and MAPE, and write a short summary of your model choice and results.

**Lecture 256 Extra practice: ARIMA vs exponential smoothing comparison drill**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Time Series + Recommendation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Directly compare ARIMA and exponential smoothing on the same series to build intuition for when each model family tends to outperform the other.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Additional depth lecture (replaces this month's original duplicated content): fit both an ARIMA model (Lecture 243) and the appropriate exponential smoothing variant (Lecture 244) on the exact same time series, evaluate both using proper walk-forward validation (Lecture 245), and directly compare their RMSE and MAPE results -- building concrete, hands-on intuition for a question this month's lectures addressed only conceptually: which model family tends to win on a series with strong autocorrelation structure versus one with clean, simple trend-and-seasonality structure. |
| **Worked example**      | Fitting both model types on a series with a clean, dominant yearly seasonal pattern and relatively weak autocorrelation might show Holt-Winters outperforming ARIMA, while a series with strong short-term autocorrelation and a less regular seasonal pattern might favour ARIMA instead -- a concrete result rather than an abstract rule.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why is directly comparing both model families on the same series, using the same validation method, more informative than reading about their theoretical differences alone?

\(A\) Reading about theoretical differences is always sufficient and direct comparison adds no real information

**(B) A head-to-head comparison on identical, fairly-validated data reveals which model family actually performs better for this specific series' real structure, rather than relying on a general rule that may not hold for every case**

\(C\) ARIMA and exponential smoothing always produce mathematically identical forecasts on any series

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Fit both an ARIMA model and an exponential smoothing model on the same time series, evaluate both with walk-forward validation, and write 3-4 sentences on which performed better and your best guess as to why, based on that series' decomposition.

**Lecture 257 Extra practice: lag-feature engineering drill**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Time Series + Recommendation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Practise engineering a richer set of lag and rolling-window features on a second, independent time series to build fluency through repetition.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Additional depth lecture (replaces this month's original duplicated content): repeat Lecture 246's lag-feature and rolling-statistic engineering on a second, different time series dataset, this time engineering a slightly larger feature set (at least 3 different lag periods and 2 different rolling window sizes) and training a standard regression model on the result, reinforcing the pattern until the habit of checking for future-data leakage in every engineered feature becomes automatic. |
| **Worked example**      | A website-traffic dataset (different from whatever series was used in Lecture 246) gains \`lag_1\`, \`lag_7\`, and \`lag_28\` columns alongside 7-day and 28-day rolling means, all verified to reference only data strictly before each row's own date before a gradient boosting model is trained on the result.                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why is repeating this lag-engineering exercise on a second, independent dataset valuable rather than redundant with Lecture 246?

\(A\) Repetition never adds any value once a technique has been demonstrated a single time

**(B) Applying the same careful process to new, unfamiliar data builds the habit of checking for leakage automatically, rather than only being able to do it correctly when following a familiar worked example**

\(C\) A second dataset always requires a completely different feature engineering approach with no overlap

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** On a time series dataset different from the one used in Lecture 246, engineer at least 3 lag features and 2 rolling-window features, train a regression model on the result, and verify no feature leaks future information.

**Lecture 258 Extra practice: collaborative filtering drill**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Time Series + Recommendation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a second, independent collaborative filtering recommender on a different dataset to deepen fluency with user-item similarity computation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | Additional depth lecture (replaces this month's original duplicated content): construct a new user-item interaction matrix from a different domain than Lecture 250's example (e.g. music, books, or restaurants instead of whatever was used there), implement both user-based and item-based collaborative filtering on it this time (rather than just one, as in Lecture 250), and compare the top recommendations each variant produces for the same target user, building direct intuition for how the two variants can genuinely disagree on a real, if small, dataset. |
| **Worked example**      | A restaurant recommendation matrix built from 6 users and 10 restaurants might show user-based filtering recommending a restaurant liked by a single very-similar user, while item-based filtering recommends a different restaurant that's broadly similar across many users' patterns to one the target user already rated highly -- a concrete illustration of the two methods' genuinely different mechanics.                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** What is the most direct way to confirm, hands-on, that user-based and item-based collaborative filtering are genuinely different methods rather than just two names for the same computation?

\(A\) Reading their definitions is always sufficient; implementing both is unnecessary

**(B) Implementing both methods on the same matrix and directly comparing their resulting recommendations, since they can produce different top recommendations for the same user from the same data**

\(C\) User-based and item-based filtering are mathematically guaranteed to always produce identical recommendations

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Build a new user-item interaction matrix (at least 6 users, 10 items) from a domain different from Lecture 250's example, implement both user-based and item-based collaborative filtering on it, and compare each variant's top-2 recommendations for one target user.

**Lecture 259 Extra practice: forecast evaluation drill**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Time Series + Recommendation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Practise computing and interpreting RMSE, MAPE and a naive-baseline comparison together to judge whether a forecasting model provides genuine value.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | Additional depth lecture (replaces this month's original duplicated content): beyond simply computing RMSE and MAPE (Lecture 248) for a model, this drill adds the single most important sanity check in forecasting evaluation that's easy to skip -- comparing the model's error against a naive baseline forecast (such as "tomorrow will equal today" or "this month will equal the same month last year"), since a sophisticated model that fails to beat even this trivial baseline has not actually demonstrated real forecasting value, however reasonable its RMSE or MAPE number looks in isolation. |
| **Worked example**      | A carefully tuned ARIMA model reporting a MAPE of 12% sounds reasonable in isolation, but discovering that a naive "same value as last week" baseline achieves an 11% MAPE on the same data reveals the sophisticated model has added essentially no real forecasting value over doing nothing at all.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** Why is comparing a forecasting model's error against a naive baseline forecast an essential step, rather than simply reporting the model's RMSE or MAPE on its own?

\(A\) A standalone RMSE or MAPE number always proves a model has genuine forecasting value with no further comparison needed

**(B) A model's error number only demonstrates genuine value when it meaningfully beats a trivial naive baseline; otherwise a seemingly reasonable error number can mask a model that adds nothing over doing nothing at all**

\(C\) Naive baseline forecasts can never be computed for real-world time series data

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For one of your earlier forecasting models, compute a naive baseline forecast (same value as the previous period, or the same period last season), calculate its RMSE and MAPE, and compare those numbers directly against your model's results to state whether your model genuinely adds value.
