**Lecture 329 Text preprocessing, revisited**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Review and extend Year 1's text preprocessing (tokenisation, normalisation) as the foundation for this month's NLP work.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Earlier text preprocessing covered lowercasing, punctuation removal, and splitting text into tokens (words); this lecture reviews that foundation and extends it with practical considerations that matter once you build real NLP models -- handling contractions, numbers, and special characters consistently, and recognising that over-aggressive normalisation (e.g. stripping all punctuation from code snippets or social media text) can destroy meaning the model actually needs. Every technique from Lecture 330 onward (subword tokenisation, embeddings, classifiers) assumes this preprocessing foundation is already solid. |
| **Worked example**      | Lowercasing "Apple" the company name the same as "apple" the fruit can blur a genuinely useful distinction in some tasks, so the right preprocessing always depends on what the downstream model actually needs to know.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why can aggressive text preprocessing (e.g. stripping all punctuation and lowercasing everything) sometimes hurt rather than help a downstream NLP model?

\(A\) Preprocessing always improves every NLP model with no exceptions

**(B) It can destroy information the model actually needs to distinguish meaning (e.g. casing that distinguishes a company name from a common word), depending on the task**

\(C\) Models cannot process lowercase text at all

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Take a short paragraph of real text and preprocess it two different ways (aggressive vs. light normalisation), and write 2 sentences on what information each version preserves or loses.

**Lecture 330 Subword tokenisation**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain how subword tokenisation methods such as byte-pair encoding (BPE) work, and why modern NLP moved beyond whole-word tokenisation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Whole-word tokenisation struggles with rare or unseen words (any word not in the training vocabulary becomes an unknown token, losing all information), and requires a huge vocabulary to cover a language's full range of words; byte-pair encoding instead starts from individual characters and iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent pairs into larger subword units, building a fixed-size vocabulary of common whole words, word pieces and individual characters -- so any input, including a word never seen during training, can still be represented as a sequence of known subword pieces. This is exactly the tokenisation approach underlying the transformer models you will study in Month 21. |
| **Worked example**      | The rare word "unhappiness" might be split by BPE into subword pieces like "un", "happi", "ness" -- each a known vocabulary piece -- rather than becoming a single unknown-word token the way whole-word tokenisation would treat it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** What specific problem does byte-pair encoding solve that whole-word tokenisation struggles with?

\(A\) It makes text preprocessing completely unnecessary

**(B) It can represent rare or previously unseen words as sequences of known subword pieces, instead of mapping them to a single unknown-word token**

\(C\) It eliminates the need for a vocabulary of any kind

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Look up (or run) a BPE tokeniser on 3 words of your choice, including at least one uncommon or made-up word, and record how each is split into subword pieces.

**Lecture 331 Word embeddings: word2vec and GloVe concepts**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain how word embeddings represent words as dense vectors that capture semantic meaning, and why this is an improvement over simple word identifiers.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | A word embedding represents each word as a dense vector of real numbers (commonly 100-300 dimensions) learned so that words appearing in similar contexts end up with similar vectors; word2vec learns these vectors by training a shallow network to predict a word from its surrounding context (or vice versa), while GloVe learns them from global word co-occurrence statistics across a whole corpus -- both approaches, trained purely on raw text with no manual labelling, famously capture meaningful relationships such as vector("king") - vector("man") + vector("woman") landing close to vector("queen"). |
| **Worked example**      | In a trained word2vec embedding space, the vectors for "dog" and "puppy" end up close together (similar contexts), while "dog" and "bicycle" end up far apart -- despite no human ever labelling any word with a meaning category.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** What makes word embeddings like word2vec or GloVe more useful to a model than representing each word with an arbitrary unique ID number?

\(A\) Embeddings take up less storage space than ID numbers

**(B) Embeddings place semantically similar words close together in vector space, letting a model generalise based on meaning rather than treating every word as totally unrelated to every other**

\(C\) Arbitrary ID numbers cannot be stored by a computer

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Load a pretrained word embedding set (e.g. via a library like gensim) and find the 5 words with vectors closest to a word of your choice, checking whether they are semantically related.

**Lecture 332 Bag-of-words and TF-IDF baselines**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build bag-of-words and TF-IDF text representations and explain why they remain useful baselines despite ignoring word order.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Bag-of-words represents a document as a vector of raw word counts, completely ignoring word order and grammar; TF-IDF (term frequency-inverse document frequency) improves on this by down-weighting words that appear in nearly every document (like "the") and up-weighting words that are frequent in one document but rare across the whole corpus, making them more informative for distinguishing documents. Despite ignoring order entirely -- a real limitation plain bag-of-words and TF-IDF share -- both remain genuinely useful, fast, simple baselines to compare any more complex neural NLP model (Lecture 333 onward) against, so you know whether the added complexity is actually earning its keep. |
| **Worked example**      | Classifying news articles by topic (sports vs. finance vs. politics) often works surprisingly well with just TF-IDF features, since topic-indicating words ("touchdown," "earnings," "election") carry most of the needed signal even without considering their order in the sentence.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why does TF-IDF down-weight extremely common words like "the" or "and" compared to plain word-count bag-of-words?

\(A\) Because common words are always misspelled in real text

**(B) Because a word appearing in nearly every document carries little information for distinguishing one document from another, so TF-IDF's inverse-document-frequency term reduces its weight**

\(C\) Because TF-IDF cannot process common words at all

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Build TF-IDF features for a small set of 5-10 short text documents of your choice, and identify which words end up with the highest TF-IDF weight in one specific document.

**Lecture 333 RNNs and LSTMs for sequential text**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain how recurrent neural networks and LSTMs process text as an ordered sequence, and why LSTMs address RNNs' difficulty with long-range dependencies.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | A recurrent neural network (RNN) processes a sequence one token at a time, maintaining a hidden state that is updated at each step and carries information forward -- naturally suited to text, unlike bag-of-words, since word order directly affects the hidden state. However, plain RNNs struggle to retain information across many steps because of the same vanishing-gradient problem from Month 17 and Lecture 317, so information from early in a long sequence tends to fade out before it can influence a much later prediction; the LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) architecture adds a separate memory cell with learned gates controlling what to keep, forget, and output at each step, letting it retain relevant information over much longer sequences than a plain RNN can. |
| **Worked example**      | In the sentence "The book, which I bought from the small shop near my old apartment last year, was excellent," a plain RNN may have trouble carrying "book" all the way to "was excellent" across so many intervening words, while an LSTM's memory cell is specifically designed to preserve exactly that kind of long-range connection.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** What specific limitation of plain RNNs does the LSTM architecture's memory cell and gating mechanism address?

\(A\) RNNs cannot process text of any length at all

**(B) Plain RNNs struggle to retain information across long sequences due to vanishing gradients; LSTMs use gates to selectively retain or forget information over much longer ranges**

\(C\) LSTMs eliminate the need for word embeddings entirely

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write 3-4 sentences in your own words explaining, using a concrete sentence example, why remembering something from early in a long sentence can be hard for a plain RNN.

**Lecture 334 Introduction to the attention mechanism**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain the core idea behind the attention mechanism: letting a model directly weigh and combine information from every position in a sequence, previewing Month 21's transformers.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Rather than forcing all of a sequence's information to pass through a single hidden state step-by-step as an RNN does, the attention mechanism lets the model, at each position, compute a weighted combination of information from every other position in the sequence directly, with the weights themselves learned to reflect how relevant each other position is to the current one. This directly solves the long-range-dependency struggle from Lecture 333 -- distant tokens are no longer diluted through many sequential steps, since attention can connect any two positions directly regardless of distance -- and is the foundational idea Month 21 builds into the full transformer architecture. |
| **Worked example**      | In the sentence "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big," attention lets the model directly connect "it" to "suitcase" (the correct referent here) regardless of how many words sit in between, rather than relying on that connection surviving step-by-step through an RNN's hidden state.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** How does attention address the long-range-dependency challenge that RNNs and LSTMs face?

\(A\) By simply increasing the model's number of layers

**(B) By allowing a direct, learned connection between any two positions in a sequence, rather than requiring information to pass step-by-step through intermediate positions**

\(C\) By ignoring word order completely, like bag-of-words does

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick one sentence with a pronoun referring to an earlier noun, and write out, in your own words, which other word(s) in the sentence attention would most likely need to connect that pronoun to.

**Lecture 335 What NVIDIA's Deep Learning Institute (DLI) is**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe accurately what NVIDIA's Deep Learning Institute is and how its training offerings are structured.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | NVIDIA's Deep Learning Institute (DLI) is NVIDIA's own training arm, offering hands-on, GPU-accelerated courses covering deep learning, data science, accelerated computing and related topics, delivered as self-paced online courses or instructor-led workshops; unlike a certification such as Azure's AI-901 (Month 9) which is a single proctored, pass/fail multiple-choice exam, DLI courses are completed by working through structured, cloud-hosted hands-on labs and exercises, and successful completion of a course earns a certificate of competency in that specific course's topic -- there is no single overarching "DLI exam" to sit. Several DLI courses relate directly to this program's deep learning and NLP content, making them a natural way to add verifiable, hands-on practice to a portfolio. |
| **Worked example**      | A learner completing NVIDIA's DLI course on "Fundamentals of Deep Learning" works through GPU-accelerated Jupyter-notebook-based labs inside NVIDIA's cloud environment, and on finishing the course's required labs, receives a certificate of competency specific to that course -- not a pass/fail score on a single timed exam.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** How does earning a DLI certificate differ structurally from earning a certification like Azure's AI-901?

\(A\) They are identical: both require passing one proctored, timed multiple-choice exam

**(B) A DLI certificate is earned by completing a specific course's hands-on, GPU-accelerated labs, rather than by passing a single proctored pass/fail exam**

\(C\) DLI certificates require no coursework of any kind and are issued automatically

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Browse NVIDIA's Deep Learning Institute course catalogue online and list 2 course titles relevant to NLP or deep learning, noting each course's stated format (self-paced vs. instructor-led).

**Lecture 337 Building an NLP text classifier, hands-on**

This directly builds the technical core of this month's NLP classifier project. |
| **Worked example**      | Training both a TF-IDF-plus-logistic-regression classifier and an LSTM-based classifier on the same 3-class news headline dataset, and comparing their validation accuracy to see whether the LSTM's sequence-awareness earns a meaningful improvement over the simpler baseline.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

\(A\) Because TF-IDF models are always more accurate than neural models

**(B) Because comparing against a simple, fast baseline tells you whether the added complexity of the neural approach is actually earning a meaningful accuracy improvement on this specific dataset**

\(C\) Because neural models cannot process text data at all

***Correct answer: B***

**Lecture 338 Evaluating NLP models**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Evaluate a text classifier using accuracy, precision/recall/F1, and qualitative error inspection appropriate to text data.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | The classification evaluation metrics from Month 9 (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix) apply directly to text classifiers, and remain just as important here: a text dataset with imbalanced classes (e.g. far more neutral reviews than negative ones) can produce misleadingly high accuracy from a model that mostly predicts the majority class. Beyond the metrics, reading a sample of specific misclassified text examples is especially valuable for NLP, since it often reveals concrete, fixable causes -- sarcasm, negation ("not bad" being misread as negative), or domain-specific vocabulary the model never saw in training. |
| **Worked example**      | A sentiment classifier that reports 85% overall accuracy on an imbalanced dataset turns out, on inspecting its confusion matrix, to have very poor recall specifically on the rare negative-sentiment class -- a weakness overall accuracy alone had hidden.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why is reading a sample of specific misclassified text examples often especially valuable when evaluating an NLP model?

\(A\) Because metrics like precision and recall cannot be computed for text data

**(B) Because it often reveals concrete, fixable causes of error specific to text -- such as negation, sarcasm, or unfamiliar vocabulary -- that a single metric number would not explain**

\(C\) Because misclassified examples should always simply be deleted from the dataset

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Evaluate your Lecture 337 text classifier with a full confusion matrix, then read 5 of its misclassified examples and write one sentence on a likely specific cause for each.

**Lecture 339 Sequence labelling: named entity recognition**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe, at a conceptual level, how sequence labelling tasks such as named entity recognition assign a label to every token rather than one label per document.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Unlike text classification (Lecture 337), which assigns one label to a whole document, sequence labelling tasks assign a label to every individual token in a sequence; named entity recognition (NER) is the most common example, tagging each word as part of a person name, organisation, location, date, or "not an entity," and must correctly handle multi-word entities (e.g. "New" and "York" both tagged as parts of the same location entity) using a consistent tagging scheme. This lecture stays conceptual, but recognising when a real NLP problem needs per-token labelling rather than a single document-level label is a practical distinction you will apply often. |
| **Worked example**      | An NER system processing "Maria works at Google in London" tags "Maria" as a person entity, "Google" as an organisation entity, and "London" as a location entity -- three separate per-token labels within a single sentence, rather than one label for the whole sentence.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** How does a sequence labelling task like named entity recognition fundamentally differ from the text classification task built in Lecture 337?

\(A\) Sequence labelling cannot use word embeddings as input

**(B) Sequence labelling assigns a label to every individual token in the sequence, rather than a single label to the whole document**

\(C\) Sequence labelling only works on documents containing exactly one sentence

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Take 3 sentences containing at least one person, organisation, or location name each, and manually tag each word with its correct entity label (or "not an entity"), by hand.

**Lecture 340 Common NLP pitfalls**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · NLP Fundamentals + NVIDIA DLI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Identify and avoid common NLP pitfalls: vocabulary mismatch, sequence length handling, and data leakage via overlapping text.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | Several NLP-specific mistakes quietly undermine model quality: vocabulary mismatch occurs when a model trained on one domain's vocabulary (e.g. formal news text) is applied to a very different domain (e.g. casual social media text) full of words it never saw in training; sequence length handling is a practical necessity since real text varies hugely in length and must be truncated or padded to a consistent size for batch processing, with the truncation point itself a real design decision that can discard important content; and data leakage can occur when overlapping or near-duplicate text passages appear in both the training and test sets (for instance, a dataset built from the same long article split across both sets), inflating test performance in a way that does not reflect genuine generalisation. |
| **Worked example**      | A sentiment model trained entirely on formal product reviews performs poorly when deployed on casual, slang-heavy social media comments, because its training vocabulary never included most of the informal words and abbreviations the new domain actually uses.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why might a text classifier trained on one domain's text perform poorly when applied to a different domain's text, even if both domains concern the same general topic?

\(A\) Because all domains of text are identical and this should never happen

**(B) Because of vocabulary mismatch: the model's learned representations are based on the specific words and style it was trained on, which may differ substantially from the new domain's vocabulary**

\(C\) Because text classifiers can only ever process one specific sentence length

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Review an NLP dataset (yours or a public example) and check for 2 of these pitfalls specifically: inspect a sample of text lengths to see how much truncation/padding would be needed, and check for any overlapping or near-duplicate passages across train/test.

**Month 21 Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I**
