**Lecture 345 The transformer architecture: why it replaced RNNs**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain, at a high level, why the transformer architecture replaced RNNs and LSTMs as the dominant architecture for most NLP tasks.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | RNNs and LSTMs (Month 20) process a sequence strictly one token at a time, which both limits training speed (each step depends on the previous one, blocking parallelisation) and still struggles somewhat with very long-range dependencies despite LSTM's gating; the transformer, introduced in 2017, processes an entire sequence at once using self-attention (Lecture 346) to directly connect any two positions regardless of distance, which is both far more parallelisable on GPU hardware and better at capturing long-range relationships. This architectural shift is what enabled the much larger models and datasets that define modern NLP, including the models you'll use hands-on later this month. |
| **Worked example**      | Training an RNN on a long document requires processing it step by step in sequence, while a transformer can process the entire document's tokens in parallel on a GPU, dramatically speeding up training on large datasets.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** What is the primary architectural reason transformers train faster on large datasets than RNNs do?

\(A\) Transformers use fewer parameters than RNNs

**(B) Transformers process a whole sequence in parallel via self-attention, rather than being forced through RNNs' strictly sequential, step-by-step processing**

\(C\) Transformers do not require a GPU at all

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write 3-4 sentences in your own words comparing how an RNN versus a transformer would process the same 20-word sentence, focusing on what can happen in parallel.

**Lecture 346 Self-attention: queries, keys and values**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain mechanically how self-attention computes, for each token, a weighted combination of all other tokens using learned query, key and value vectors.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | For each input token, self-attention computes three vectors via learned projections: a query (what this token is looking for), a key (what this token offers to others), and a value (the actual information this token contributes); a token's query is compared against every token's key (via a dot product) to produce attention scores, which are normalised (via softmax) into weights, and the token's new representation becomes the weighted sum of all tokens' value vectors using those weights. This is the precise mechanical version of the attention idea previewed conceptually in Month 20, Lecture 334. |
| **Worked example**      | When processing "it" in "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big," the query vector for "it" produces a high attention score against the key vector for "suitcase," so "suitcase"'s value vector contributes heavily to "it"'s new representation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** In self-attention, what determines how much one token's value vector contributes to another token's new representation?

\(A\) The two tokens' positions in the vocabulary list, alphabetically

**(B) The attention weight produced by comparing the receiving token's query vector against the contributing token's key vector**

\(C\) Whether the two tokens have exactly the same word embedding

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick one short sentence and, for one specific token in it, write down (in plain English, not vectors) which other tokens you'd expect a well-trained query/key comparison to assign the highest attention weight to, and why.

**Lecture 347 Multi-head attention**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain why transformers run several attention computations in parallel (multiple heads) rather than just one.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | A single self-attention computation learns one specific pattern of relationships between tokens; multi-head attention runs several independent attention computations (heads) in parallel, each with its own learned query/key/value projections, allowing different heads to specialise in capturing different kinds of relationships simultaneously -- one head might learn to track grammatical subject-verb agreement while another tracks coreference (like the "it"/"suitcase" link from Lecture 346) -- and the heads' outputs are then concatenated and combined into a single result. |
| **Worked example**      | In a trained transformer, one attention head might consistently focus on each verb's grammatical subject, while a different head in the same layer focuses on tracking pronoun references back to the nouns they refer to -- two different relationship types captured in parallel within the same layer.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a transformer use multiple attention heads rather than one larger single attention computation?

\(A\) To reduce the model's total number of parameters

**(B) So that different heads can specialise in capturing different kinds of token relationships in parallel, rather than being limited to one single learned pattern**

\(C\) Because a single attention computation cannot be run on a GPU

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Research (via a diagram or article) how many attention heads a well-known transformer model such as the original BERT-base uses per layer, and write down that number.

**Lecture 348 Positional encoding**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain why transformers need an explicit positional encoding, given that self-attention alone has no inherent notion of token order.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Unlike an RNN, which processes tokens strictly in sequence and so has order built directly into its processing, self-attention computes relationships between all token pairs simultaneously and would treat "the dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog" as the exact same set of tokens with no way to distinguish their different orderings; positional encoding solves this by adding a position-dependent signal (commonly based on sine and cosine functions of varying frequencies) to each token's embedding before it enters the self-attention layers, giving the model the order information it would otherwise completely lack. |
| **Worked example**      | Without positional encoding, a transformer processing the words "the," "dog," "bit," "the," "man" would have no way to distinguish this from the words in any other order, since self-attention alone treats the input as an unordered set of tokens.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a transformer require an explicit positional encoding, while an RNN does not need one?

\(A\) Transformers cannot process more than one token at a time without it

**(B) Self-attention computes relationships between all token pairs at once with no inherent sense of sequence order, unlike an RNN's inherently sequential, order-preserving processing**

\(C\) Positional encoding is only needed for very short sentences

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write 2-3 sentences explaining, in your own words, what would likely go wrong if positional encoding were removed from a trained transformer model.

**Lecture 349 The encoder-decoder structure**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe the original transformer's encoder-decoder structure and the task (sequence-to-sequence, such as translation) it was originally designed for.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | The original transformer paper used an encoder-decoder structure: the encoder processes the full input sequence (e.g. an English sentence) into a rich contextual representation using self-attention, and the decoder generates the output sequence (e.g. the French translation) one token at a time, attending both to its own previously generated tokens and to the encoder's output via a separate cross-attention mechanism. This structure suits sequence-to-sequence tasks where the output is a genuinely different sequence from the input; Lectures 350-351 cover two major simplified variants that each use only one half of this structure for different purposes. |
| **Worked example**      | A machine translation transformer's encoder reads the full English sentence "the cat sat down" into contextual representations, and its decoder then generates the French output "le chat s'est assis" one word at a time, referring back to the encoder's representations at each step.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** What distinguishes the original transformer's decoder from its encoder in terms of what each attends to?

\(A\) The decoder only attends to the input; the encoder only attends to the output

**(B) The decoder attends both to its own previously generated output tokens and to the encoder's representations of the input, via cross-attention**

\(C\) The encoder and decoder are functionally identical with no difference

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick a sequence-to-sequence task other than translation (e.g. text summarisation) and describe in 2-3 sentences what would play the role of the encoder's input and the decoder's output.

**Lecture 350 Encoder-only models: BERT**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe what BERT-style encoder-only models are good at, and why their bidirectional pretraining suits understanding tasks rather than text generation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) uses only the encoder half of the transformer, pretrained with a masked-language-modelling objective: random tokens in a sentence are hidden, and the model must predict them using context from both the left and the right simultaneously (true bidirectionality, unlike a left-to-right-only model), producing a deeply contextual representation of each token that is excellent for understanding tasks -- classification, question answering, named entity recognition (Month 20, Lecture 339) -- but awkward for generating new text one token at a time, since BERT was never trained to predict what comes next in sequence. |
| **Worked example**      | Fine-tuning a pretrained BERT model on a sentiment classification task typically needs only a small amount of labelled data and a few epochs, since BERT's pretrained bidirectional representations already encode rich general language understanding.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why is BERT well-suited to classification and question-answering tasks but poorly suited to open-ended text generation?

\(A\) BERT was pretrained to predict masked tokens using full bidirectional context, which builds strong understanding representations but was never trained to generate text one token at a time in sequence

**(B) BERT has no attention mechanism at all**

\(C\) BERT can only process single words, never full sentences

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Look up one real application that uses a BERT-style model and identify whether it is a classification, question-answering, or similar understanding task (not text generation).

**Lecture 351 Decoder-only models: GPT-style**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe what GPT-style decoder-only models are good at, and why their left-to-right pretraining suits text generation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | GPT-style models use only the decoder half of the transformer (without the encoder or cross-attention), pretrained with a next-token-prediction objective: given all tokens so far, predict the next one, using only left-to-right context (masked so a position cannot attend to tokens that come after it) -- a training objective that directly matches how text is generated at inference time, one token at a time, each new token conditioned on everything generated before it. This makes decoder-only models naturally suited to open-ended generation (chat, completion, summarisation phrased as generation) though, unlike BERT, each token's representation only ever sees context to its left. |
| **Worked example**      | A GPT-style model generating a story continues one word at a time, each new word chosen based on every word generated so far, exactly matching the left-to-right next-token-prediction objective it was pretrained on.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why does GPT-style pretraining (next-token prediction, left-to-right only) match text generation particularly well?

\(A\) Because next-token prediction is identical to BERT's masked-token prediction

**(B) Because generation itself happens one token at a time conditioned only on what came before, which is exactly the task the model was pretrained to perform**

\(C\) Because GPT-style models do not use the attention mechanism

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write 2-3 sentences comparing BERT's masked, bidirectional pretraining objective to GPT's next-token, left-to-right pretraining objective, in your own words.

**Lecture 352 Pretraining vs. fine-tuning for transformers**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Distinguish a transformer's pretraining phase from its fine-tuning phase, and explain why this two-stage approach is so effective.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Pretraining is a long, expensive, general-purpose phase where a transformer learns broad language patterns from a massive, unlabelled text corpus using a self-supervised objective (masked-token prediction for BERT-style, next-token prediction for GPT-style) that requires no human labelling at all; fine-tuning then takes that pretrained model and continues training it, much more briefly, on a smaller labelled dataset for a specific downstream task, adjusting the general-purpose representations toward the task at hand. This mirrors the transfer learning idea from Month 19's computer vision content (Lecture 319), and is precisely why a team with only a few thousand labelled examples can still reach strong performance by starting from a transformer pretrained on billions of words. |
| **Worked example**      | A team with only 2,000 labelled customer support tickets fine-tunes a transformer that was pretrained on a huge general text corpus, reaching strong classification accuracy that training the same architecture from scratch on just 2,000 examples could never achieve.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why can fine-tuning achieve strong performance with a relatively small labelled dataset, when training the same architecture from scratch on that same small dataset would not?

\(A\) Because fine-tuning uses a completely different, simpler architecture

**(B) Because pretraining has already taught the model broad, general language patterns from a massive corpus, so fine-tuning only needs to adjust toward the specific task rather than learn language from nothing**

\(C\) Because small datasets always produce better results than large ones

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write 2-3 sentences explaining, in your own words, why pretraining can use unlabelled text while fine-tuning requires labelled examples.

**Lecture 353 Transfer learning with transformers**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply the transfer-learning concept specifically to transformers: choosing between using a pretrained model's features directly versus fully fine-tuning its weights.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | As with Month 19's CNN backbones, a pretrained transformer can be used in more than one way: as a frozen feature extractor (its weights are not updated; only a small new classification head is trained on top of its fixed output representations -- fast and cheap but less flexible), or fully fine-tuned (some or all of the pretrained weights are also updated during training on the new task -- typically more accurate but more expensive and more prone to overfitting on a very small dataset). The right choice depends on dataset size, available compute, and how different the new task is from what the model was pretrained on, exactly the same judgment call Month 19 introduced for vision backbones. |
| **Worked example**      | With only a few hundred labelled examples, freezing a pretrained transformer's weights and training only a small classification head on top is often safer than fully fine-tuning, since full fine-tuning risks overfitting such a tiny dataset.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** When might freezing a pretrained transformer's weights (using it only as a feature extractor) be preferable to fully fine-tuning it?

\(A\) Always; frozen features are strictly better in every situation

**(B) When the labelled dataset is very small, since full fine-tuning on very little data risks overfitting the pretrained weights to too few examples**

\(C\) Never; frozen features cannot be used for any real task

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For a task and dataset size of your choice, decide and justify in 2-3 sentences whether you would freeze the pretrained transformer's weights or fully fine-tune it.

**Lecture 354 Introduction to the Hugging Face ecosystem**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe the core components of the Hugging Face ecosystem -- pretrained models, tokenizers, and pipelines -- and how they fit together.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Hugging Face provides a widely-used open-source ecosystem for working with transformers: the Model Hub hosts thousands of pretrained models (BERT, GPT-style, and many task-specific fine-tuned variants) ready to download; each model ships with a matching tokenizer implementing the exact subword tokenisation (Month 20, Lecture 330) that model expects; and the high-level \`pipeline\` API wraps model loading, tokenisation, inference, and output post-processing into a few lines of code for common tasks like sentiment analysis or text generation. Together these pieces make trying a state-of-the-art pretrained transformer dramatically faster than building the infrastructure to do so from scratch. |
| **Worked example**      | Running \`pipeline("sentiment-analysis")\` in a few lines of Python downloads a pretrained model and its matching tokenizer, and returns a usable sentiment classifier immediately -- work that would otherwise require manually assembling model architecture, pretrained weights, and tokenisation logic.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why must a Hugging Face model always be paired with its own specific matching tokenizer, rather than any tokenizer being interchangeable?

\(A\) Tokenizers are purely cosmetic and have no effect on a model's output

**(B) A model was trained on text tokenised a specific way (a specific subword vocabulary and scheme); feeding it text tokenised differently would not match what it learned to expect as input**

\(C\) All Hugging Face models share one universal tokenizer

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Install the Hugging Face transformers library (or review its documentation) and identify the name of one pretrained model and its matching tokenizer for a task of your choice.

**Lecture 355 Using a pretrained transformer for a task, hands-on**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Use a pretrained transformer model to perform a real NLP task directly, with no training required.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Hands-on lecture: using Hugging Face's \`pipeline\` API (Lecture 354), apply a pretrained transformer to a real task -- sentiment analysis, text summarisation, or question answering -- on your own example inputs, with no training step at all, and inspect the output's structure (label, confidence score, or generated text) to understand exactly what the pretrained model returns. This demonstrates directly how much capability a pretrained transformer already provides before any task-specific fine-tuning (Lecture 356) is even applied. |
| **Worked example**      | Feeding a customer review into a pretrained sentiment-analysis pipeline immediately returns a label ("POSITIVE" or "NEGATIVE") and a confidence score, with zero training performed -- purely from the model's pretrained and (for this specific pipeline) already task-fine-tuned weights.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Using a pretrained sentiment-analysis pipeline out of the box, with no additional training, on your own text inputs demonstrates what?

\(A\) That transformers require training before they can be used for anything at all

**(B) That a pretrained (and often already task-tuned) model can perform a real task immediately, without any additional training from the user**

\(C\) That pipelines only work on text the model was literally trained on, word for word

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Use a pretrained pipeline (sentiment analysis, summarisation, or question answering) on at least 5 of your own example inputs, and record the output for each.

**Lecture 356 Fine-tuning a transformer for a specific task, hands-on**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Fine-tune a pretrained transformer on a labelled dataset for a specific classification task.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | Hands-on lecture: take a pretrained transformer (e.g. a BERT-style model via Hugging Face), attach a classification head, and fine-tune it on a labelled dataset for a specific task (e.g. classifying support tickets or reviews), using a much smaller learning rate and far fewer epochs than training from scratch would require, exactly as the pretraining-vs-fine-tuning concept from Lecture 352 predicts. This directly builds the technical core of this month's transformer text application project, and gives firsthand experience of how much less data and training time fine-tuning needs compared to Month 20's from-scratch neural classifiers. |
| **Worked example**      | Fine-tuning a pretrained BERT model for 3 epochs on 2,000 labelled support tickets reaches strong classification accuracy that training an equivalent-sized model entirely from scratch on the same 2,000 examples could not come close to matching.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why does fine-tuning a transformer typically use a much smaller learning rate than training a model from scratch?

\(A\) Because small learning rates train models faster in every case

**(B) Because the pretrained weights already encode useful, general representations, and a small learning rate makes careful, limited adjustments toward the new task without destroying that existing knowledge**

\(C\) Because transformers cannot be trained with a large learning rate for any reason

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Fine-tune a pretrained transformer on a labelled text classification dataset of your choice, recording its validation accuracy and the number of epochs used.

**Lecture 357 Evaluating a fine-tuned transformer**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Evaluate a fine-tuned transformer using the same rigorous evaluation practices applied throughout this program, adapted to transformer-specific considerations.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Evaluating a fine-tuned transformer uses the same core tools as any classifier (accuracy, precision/recall/F1, confusion matrix, Month 9 and Month 20) plus transformer-specific considerations: checking performance doesn't degrade on inputs longer than what the model typically saw during fine-tuning, confirming the fine-tuned model actually outperforms a simpler baseline (reusing the comparison habit from Month 20, Lecture 337) to justify the much larger model's added cost, and inspecting misclassified examples for patterns (ambiguous phrasing, domain-specific vocabulary the model never saw) exactly as in Month 20, Lecture 338. |
| **Worked example**      | A fine-tuned transformer reaches 94% accuracy versus a TF-IDF baseline's 88% on the same dataset -- a real but modest improvement that a team might reasonably weigh against the transformer's much higher training and inference cost before deciding which to deploy.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why is comparing a fine-tuned transformer's accuracy against a simpler baseline's accuracy an important part of evaluating it, rather than just reporting the transformer's accuracy alone?

\(A\) Because transformers always perform worse than simple baselines, so this check is purely a formality

**(B) Because it reveals whether the transformer's substantially higher computational cost is actually justified by a meaningful accuracy improvement over the simpler, cheaper alternative**

\(C\) Because simple baselines cannot be evaluated using the same metrics as transformers

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Evaluate your Lecture 356 fine-tuned transformer with a full confusion matrix, and compare its accuracy against a simple baseline (e.g. TF-IDF-based) on the same dataset and task.

**Lecture 358 Transformer text application: building the project (part 1)**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| **Teacher explanation** | Project lecture, part 1: choose a real NLP task for the application (e.g. a review sentiment classifier, a support-ticket router, or a question-answering tool over a small document set), select an appropriate pretrained transformer from the Hugging Face ecosystem (Lecture 354) for that task, and either apply it directly (Lecture 355) or fine-tune it on a labelled dataset (Lecture 356) depending on whether an off-the-shelf pretrained model already fits the task closely enough -- establishing the working model that part 2 will evaluate and finish into a complete application. |

**Knowledge check:** When starting this project, how should you decide between using a pretrained model directly versus fine-tuning it?

\(A\) Always fine-tune, regardless of whether an existing pretrained pipeline already fits the task

**(B) Check whether an existing pretrained pipeline already closely matches the specific task and labels needed; if not, fine-tuning on your own labelled data becomes necessary**

**Lecture 359 Transformer text application: evaluating and finishing the project (part 2)**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · Transformers + IBM AI Engineering I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Complete the month's transformer text application by evaluating it rigorously, comparing against a baseline, and wrapping it in a usable interface or API.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Before finalising this project, why should the fine-tuned transformer's performance be explicitly compared against a simpler baseline rather than deployed on its own metrics alone?

\(A\) Because baselines are required by Hugging Face's software licence

**(B) Because it demonstrates the transformer's added complexity and cost is actually justified by a genuine performance improvement, rather than assuming bigger always means better**

\(C\) Because the transformer's own metrics cannot be trusted without a baseline present

**Lecture 360 IBM AI Engineering: program structure and the machine-learning-with-Python course**

**Lecture 369 End-to-end AI service architecture**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · IBM AI Engineering II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe the three core layers of an end-to-end AI service: the model, the API layer, and the client.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | An end-to-end AI service typically has three layers: a trained model that does the actual prediction, an API layer (built in Month 16, e.g. with FastAPI) that wraps the model in HTTP endpoints, and a client -- a simple front-end, command-line tool, or another program -- that calls those endpoints and does something useful with the result; keeping these layers cleanly separated makes each one independently testable and replaceable. |
| **Worked example**      | A sentiment-analysis service has a trained classifier (model layer), a \`/predict\` FastAPI endpoint wrapping it (API layer), and a small web form where a user types text and sees the result (client layer) -- any layer can be swapped without touching the others.                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why is it valuable to keep the model, API, and client layers of a service cleanly separated?

\(A\) Separation makes the service slower and should be avoided

**(B) Each layer can be tested, updated, or replaced independently without requiring changes to the other layers**

\(C\) Separation is only a stylistic preference with no practical benefit

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Sketch (on paper or in a text file) the three-layer architecture for an AI service idea of your own, naming what each layer would actually do.

**Lecture 370 Service orchestration basics**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · IBM AI Engineering II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain, at an introductory level, how multiple components of an AI service communicate and coordinate with each other.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Orchestration refers to how a service's separate components -- the API layer, a database, a model-serving process, perhaps a queue -- are coordinated so requests flow through them in the right order and failures in one component don't silently corrupt another; even a simple two-component service (API calling a model) is a minimal form of orchestration, and this concept scales up directly into Month 23's container-orchestration content. |
| **Worked example**      | In a service where the API layer receives a request, calls the model component for a prediction, then writes the result to a log before responding, the API layer is acting as the orchestrator coordinating those three steps in sequence.                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** In a simple AI service where an API calls a model and then logs the result, which component is acting as the orchestrator of that sequence?

\(A\) The model, because it does the prediction

**(B) The API layer, because it coordinates the order in which the model call and the logging happen**

\(C\) Orchestration doesn't apply to services with only two components

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Diagram the order of operations (as a numbered list) for a 3-step service request in an app you're familiar with, identifying which component coordinates the steps.

**Lecture 371 Integrating a third-party AI API as a service component**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · IBM AI Engineering II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain how to incorporate an external AI API (e.g. a cloud provider's NLP or vision endpoint) as one component inside a larger original service.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Rather than always training your own model, a production AI service component can legitimately be a call out to a third-party API (as introduced conceptually with cloud AI services in Month 9) -- the engineering skill is wrapping that external call behind your own internal interface, so your service's other code doesn't need to know or care whether a prediction came from your own model or a vendor's, and so the vendor can be swapped later with minimal disruption. |
| **Worked example**      | A service's internal \`get_sentiment(text)\` function might call a third-party sentiment API today and a locally trained model next year, with no other part of the codebase needing to change.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why should a call to a third-party AI API be wrapped behind your own internal function rather than called directly throughout your codebase?

\(A\) Third-party APIs cannot be called from Python

**(B) Wrapping it isolates the rest of the code from vendor-specific details, so the vendor can be swapped or the call modified in one place**

\(C\) Direct calls are always faster than wrapped calls

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick a free-tier third-party AI API and write a short function that wraps one call to it behind a simple, vendor-agnostic function signature (pseudocode is fine if you don't have a key).

**Lecture 372 Designing for reliability: handling failed inference**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · IBM AI Engineering II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design graceful failure handling for the moment a model's inference call fails or returns an unusable result.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | A production AI service must assume inference will sometimes fail -- a malformed input, a timeout, a model returning a low-confidence or nonsensical result -- and respond with a clear, structured error or fallback rather than crashing the whole request; this typically means wrapping the inference call in error handling, validating output shape/range before returning it, and returning an informative status code rather than a raw stack trace. |
| **Worked example**      | Instead of letting an unhandled exception crash the whole API process when the model receives malformed input, the endpoint catches the error and returns a structured \`{"error": "invalid input format"}\` response with an appropriate HTTP status code.                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** What should a well-designed AI service endpoint do when the underlying model's inference call fails?

\(A\) Let the whole service process crash so the error is obvious

**(B) Catch the failure and return a clear, structured error response, keeping the rest of the service running**

\(C\) Silently return a random prediction instead of an error

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Add a try/except (or equivalent) around a model inference call in one of your earlier API projects, and return a structured error response on failure.

**Lecture 373 Logging and basic observability for an AI service**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · IBM AI Engineering II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Implement basic logging that records what an AI service did for each request, enabling later debugging and monitoring.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Observability starts with logging: recording, for each request, at minimum a timestamp, the input (or its shape/summary), the output, how long inference took, and whether an error occurred -- without this, diagnosing a production issue days later is close to impossible, and this logging becomes the raw material Month 24 builds real monitoring dashboards from. |
| **Worked example**      | A log line like \`2026-10-14T09:03:11Z \| /predict \| latency=42ms \| status=200 \| input_len=128\` lets an engineer later answer "was the service slow at 9am?" without having to reproduce the issue.                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why is per-request logging considered foundational to observability, rather than an optional nice-to-have?

\(A\) Logging has no connection to debugging production issues

**(B) It is the raw data that later monitoring, debugging and performance analysis all depend on; without it, past behaviour is unrecoverable**

\(C\) Logging always slows a service down too much to be worthwhile

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Add basic per-request logging (timestamp, endpoint, latency, status) to one of your API projects and show 5 captured log lines.

**Lecture 377 Evaluating the end-to-end AI service project**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · IBM AI Engineering II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| **Worked example**      | A service that predicts correctly 95% of the time but crashes ungracefully on malformed input and has no logging would fail this evaluation despite its respectable accuracy, since production readiness is about more than raw accuracy.                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why does evaluating this project require more than just checking the model's prediction accuracy?

\(C\) Reliability and documentation are purely cosmetic concerns with no real impact

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

| **Learning outcome**    | Recognise common architectural and reliability mistakes students make when building their first end-to-end AI service, and how to avoid them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Frequent early mistakes include mixing model logic directly into API route handlers (making both hard to test independently), forgetting to validate input shape before passing it to the model, logging too little to debug anything useful, and skipping documentation until the very end rather than writing it alongside the build -- recognising these patterns before submitting the project catches them early. |
| **Worked example**      | A student who embeds model-loading code directly inside a FastAPI route function discovers it's now impossible to unit-test the model logic without also spinning up the whole API -- a direct consequence of not separating the layers from Lecture 369.                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why is embedding model logic directly inside an API route handler considered a common mistake?

\(A\) It is actually the recommended best practice for every service

**(B) It couples the model and API layers together, making the model logic hard to test or reuse independently of the API**

\(C\) API route handlers cannot call any other code

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Review your end-to-end AI service project against these four common mistakes and fix any you find.
