**Lecture 531 Cloud-based CI/CD for AI applications**

*Year 3 · Month 31 · Cloud AI Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Extend Year 2 Month 23's CI/CD principles with AI-specific pipeline stages: model validation, prompt regression tests, and staged rollout.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Building on Year 2's general CI/CD content, an AI application's pipeline needs stages beyond standard unit/integration tests: a model-validation stage that re-runs a fixed evaluation set against the model or prompt version being deployed and fails the build if quality metrics (accuracy, a rubric score, or a regression-test pass rate) drop below a threshold; a prompt-regression stage, since a seemingly small prompt wording change can silently break behavior on edge cases, so a suite of saved input/expected-output pairs should run on every prompt change exactly like unit tests run on every code change; and a staged-rollout stage (connecting to canary/shadow patterns covered more deeply in Month 32) where a new model or prompt version serves a small percentage of real traffic before full rollout, with automatic rollback if monitored quality or latency metrics degrade. The core principle carried over from general CI/CD -- never deploy an untested change directly to 100% of production traffic -- applies with extra force here because AI system failures (a degraded answer, a hallucination) are often silent and don't throw an error the way a crashed service does. |
| **Worked example**      | A team's CI pipeline for their support-bot prompt changes includes a 50-example golden test set; when a developer edits the prompt and the automated pass rate against that set drops from 92% to 81%, the pipeline blocks the merge automatically, catching a regression before it would have reached any real users.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why does an AI application's CI/CD pipeline need a prompt-regression test stage that a typical web application's pipeline does not?

**(A) Prompt changes can silently degrade output quality without throwing any code-level error, so only an explicit evaluation catches the regression**

\(B\) Prompts never change once written so this stage is unnecessary

\(C\) Standard unit tests already fully cover prompt quality

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design a 10-example golden test set (input + expected qualities of a good output) for one prompt-based feature, that could be run automatically on every change to that prompt.

**Lecture 532 Disaster recovery and reliability patterns for cloud AI systems**

*Year 3 · Month 31 · Cloud AI Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design disaster-recovery and reliability patterns specific to cloud AI system failure modes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Cloud AI systems have failure modes beyond typical infrastructure outages: a foundation-model provider's API can go down or get rate-limited independently of your own infrastructure, so a reliability pattern here is a fallback chain -- a secondary model provider or a smaller self-hosted model that serves degraded-but-functional responses when the primary is unavailable, with clear user-facing signaling that a fallback is active. Vector database or feature store unavailability is a second distinct failure mode, for which a graceful-degradation pattern (answering from the model's general knowledge with a caveat, rather than hard-failing the whole request) is often better than returning an error. For disaster recovery proper, this means defining a recovery point objective and recovery time objective specifically for the AI system's stateful components -- embeddings indexes, fine-tuned model weights, conversation history -- and testing that a vector index can actually be rebuilt from its source documents within the RTO, since many teams only discover their reindexing process takes 10 hours when they urgently need it to take 1. Regularly testing these failure paths (deliberately disabling the primary model provider in a staging environment) is what separates a system that has disaster recovery on paper from one that has it in practice. |
| **Worked example**      | A RAG application's primary vector database experiences an outage; instead of returning an error to every user, the application falls back to answering directly from the LLM's general knowledge with a visible "answering without document search, results may be less specific" notice, keeping the core experience partially functional.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** What distinguishes a well-designed reliability pattern for a vector-database outage from simply returning an error?

\(A\) There is no meaningful difference; an error is always the correct response

**(B) Graceful degradation keeps the system partially functional (e.g. general-knowledge answers with a caveat) rather than fully failing**

\(C\) The vector database should never be allowed to fail under any circumstances

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For one component of an AI system (model API or vector database), write a specific fallback behavior you would implement if that component became unavailable, and what the user would see.

**Lecture 533 Choosing a cloud AI architecture: a decision framework**

*Year 3 · Month 31 · Cloud AI Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply a structured decision framework to select an appropriate cloud AI architecture for a given set of requirements.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | Choosing among the architectural options covered this month (which cloud, managed vs self-hosted, serverless vs always-on, single-cloud vs abstracted) is best done with a structured framework rather than intuition: first, clarify hard constraints (data residency/compliance requirements, existing cloud commitments, team's existing skill set) which immediately rule some options out; second, estimate expected scale and traffic pattern (steady high volume favors self-hosted and always-on; bursty low-to-medium volume favors managed and serverless); third, weigh latency requirements against cost sensitivity, since the lowest-latency option is rarely the cheapest; and fourth, assess organizational risk tolerance for operational complexity, since a team of two without dedicated ops capacity should lean toward managed services even if self-hosting would technically be cheaper at their volume, because the hidden cost of an under-resourced team running its own GPU fleet is outages, not savings. Working through these four factors in order, for a specific given scenario, is the actual deliverable skill -- not memorizing a single "best" architecture, since the correct answer changes with every one of these inputs. |
| **Worked example**      | Given a scenario -- a 3-person startup, strict healthcare data residency requirements, moderate but unpredictable traffic, and no dedicated DevOps engineer -- the framework points toward: self-hosted (for residency) but on a managed Kubernetes or serverless GPU platform (to offset the lack of ops capacity) rather than raw self-managed GPU servers, illustrating how constraints can point in seemingly conflicting directions that the framework resolves by prioritizing the hard constraint first.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** In the decision framework, why are hard constraints like data residency evaluated before scale or cost considerations?

\(A\) Hard constraints are the least important factor and should be considered last

**(B) Hard constraints can eliminate otherwise-attractive options outright, so evaluating them first avoids wasted analysis on ruled-out paths**

\(C\) Scale and cost never actually matter in architecture decisions

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Apply the four-factor framework (constraints, scale, latency/cost, ops risk tolerance) to a cloud AI architecture scenario of your own choosing, and state your resulting recommendation in 3-4 sentences.

| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture begins the month's signature project: a cloud AI application built end to end incorporating this month's concepts. Part 1's deliverable is a short architecture document (modeled on lecture 523's layered approach) specifying the chosen cloud platform and justification, the managed-vs-self-hosted serving decision and why, the data/RAG layer design if applicable, the IAM and secrets approach, and the cost-management levers planned from the start rather than retrofitted later. Once the design is written, part 1 also covers setting up the actual cloud infrastructure skeleton -- the project/account structure, basic IAM roles, and a secrets store -- so that part 2's build work has a secured foundation to build on rather than starting with a wide-open default configuration that gets locked down as an afterthought. Writing the design before writing infrastructure code is the deliberate habit being reinforced: a design written after the fact tends to rationalize whatever got built rather than catching architectural mistakes early. |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture sequence writing the architecture design before provisioning any infrastructure?

\(A\) Infrastructure should always be provisioned first and designed around afterward

**(B) Writing the design first surfaces architectural mistakes early and prevents retrofitting security/cost decisions after the fact**

\(C\) The order makes no practical difference to the outcome

***Correct answer: B***

**Lecture 537 Observability as a discipline: metrics, logs, traces**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Advanced MLOps + Observability · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain the three pillars of observability and how each applies specifically to ML/LLM systems rather than generic software.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Monitoring tells you whether a known failure condition has occurred (a threshold crossed, a health check failing); observability goes further, giving you the ability to ask new questions about system behavior you didn't anticipate in advance, which matters enormously for ML/LLM systems because their failure modes are often novel and data-dependent rather than fixed error codes. The three pillars are metrics (aggregated numerical time series, e.g. requests per second, average latency, model accuracy over a rolling window), logs (discrete timestamped event records, e.g. a specific request's prompt, retrieved documents, and response), and traces (the causal chain showing how one request propagated through every component it touched, with timing at each hop). For ML/LLM systems specifically, metrics need ML-aware additions (prediction confidence distributions, drift scores), logs need careful redaction given that prompts and responses can carry sensitive user data, and traces need to capture non-obvious internal steps like a retrieval step's documents or an agent's tool calls, which a generic web-service trace would never need to record. Mastering all three pillars together, not just one, is what lets an engineer actually diagnose a confusing production incident instead of just noticing that something is wrong. |
| **Worked example**      | An engineer debugging a sudden quality complaint pulls the metrics dashboard (confirms latency is normal, so it's not a timeout issue), then the trace for one specific bad response (reveals the retrieval step returned zero documents), then the log for that step (reveals the vector database query malformed a filter), diagnosing the real root cause by moving through all three pillars in sequence.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why do ML/LLM systems need observability beyond basic uptime monitoring?

\(A\) Because uptime monitoring is sufficient for every type of system failure

**(B) Because ML/LLM failure modes (a wrong answer, drifted predictions) are often silent and data-dependent, not simple crashes a health check would catch**

\(C\) Because metrics, logs, and traces are three names for the same underlying data

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For an ML/LLM system you're familiar with (or a hypothetical one), write one example metric, one example log field, and one example trace span you'd want captured.

**Lecture 538 Distributed tracing for a multi-step AI pipeline**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Advanced MLOps + Observability · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a distributed trace for a multi-step RAG or agent pipeline that shows timing and causality across every hop.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | A RAG or agent system's single user-facing request typically fans out into many internal steps -- query embedding, vector search, document reranking, prompt assembly, the LLM call itself, and possibly one or more tool calls -- and distributed tracing captures each of these as a "span" nested under one overall "trace" representing the whole request, with each span recording its own start time, duration, and relevant metadata (e.g. the vector search span records how many documents were returned and the top similarity score). This lets an engineer immediately see, for any slow or failed request, exactly which step consumed the time or produced the bad result, rather than only knowing the total request took 4 seconds with no visibility into whether that was the embedding call, the vector search, or the LLM generation. Implementing this well requires propagating a trace ID through every internal call (including across service boundaries and into any external API call to a model provider), and recording enough span metadata to be useful without logging full document contents or full prompts into the tracing system by default, since tracing backends are often less access-controlled than application logs. A well-instrumented multi-step pipeline turns a vague "it's slow sometimes" complaint into a specific, fixable bottleneck within minutes rather than hours of guessing. |
| **Worked example**      | A trace for one RAG request shows: embed_query span (12ms), vector_search span (340ms, returned 8 documents), rerank span (45ms), llm_generate span (1,850ms) -- immediately revealing that the LLM generation step, not the retrieval pipeline, is the dominant cost and the right place to focus a latency-reduction effort.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main diagnostic advantage of distributed tracing over a single total-latency metric for a multi-step pipeline?

**(A) It shows exactly which step within the pipeline consumed the time, rather than only the opaque total**

\(B\) It removes the need to record any timing information at all

\(C\) It replaces the need for logs entirely since traces contain everything

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For a multi-step pipeline of your choice (RAG or agent), list the spans you'd instrument and what metadata (not full content) each span should record.

**Lecture 539 LLM-specific observability: tokens, cost, latency, privacy-aware logging**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Advanced MLOps + Observability · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design an LLM-specific observability layer tracking token usage, cost per request, latency breakdown, and privacy-conscious prompt/response logging.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Beyond generic service metrics, an LLM-serving system needs LLM-specific observability: token usage per request (input and output tokens separately, since they're often priced differently and output tokens reveal verbosity issues), cost per request computed from token counts and the specific model used (critical for the cost-attribution work from Month 31 and Year 2 Month 24), and a latency breakdown that separates time-to-first-token from total generation time, since these matter differently for a streaming chat UI versus a batch summarization job. Prompt and response logging is uniquely sensitive for LLM systems because prompts frequently contain user-submitted personal or confidential information, so a responsible logging design applies redaction or hashing to likely-sensitive fields, sets a strict retention window rather than indefinite storage, and restricts access to raw prompt/response logs to a small authorized group, treating this data with the same care as any other PII pipeline rather than logging it by default the way a generic HTTP request log would be. Getting this layer right from the start avoids both of the two failure modes teams commonly hit: either no visibility into cost/quality drivers at all, or a compliance problem from over-logging sensitive user content. |
| **Worked example**      | A team's LLM observability dashboard shows per-customer average tokens-per-request trending up over a month, revealing a frontend bug that was silently appending the entire conversation history to every new request instead of just the recent turns -- a cost and latency problem caught by token-usage metrics well before any user complained about slowness.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** Why does prompt/response logging for an LLM system require more care than a typical HTTP request log?

**(A) Prompts and responses frequently contain sensitive user-submitted or confidential content, requiring redaction, retention limits and access control**

\(B\) LLM logs are technically identical to any other log and need no special treatment

\(C\) Logging is unnecessary for LLM systems since metrics alone are sufficient

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design a privacy-aware logging policy for one LLM-based feature: what gets logged, what gets redacted, and the retention window you'd set.

**Lecture 540 Building alerting rules for an ML/LLM service**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Advanced MLOps + Observability · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design alerting rules for an ML/LLM service that balance sensitivity against alert fatigue.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Effective alerting for an ML/LLM service requires choosing what to alert on carefully: infrastructure-level alerts (error rate, latency percentile breaches, availability) transfer directly from general software engineering, but ML/LLM-specific alerts need new signals -- a sustained drop in a proxy quality metric (e.g. thumbs-down rate, or an automated evaluation score on sampled live traffic), a spike in token usage or cost per request, a drift score crossing a threshold (building on Year 2 Month 24's drift detection, deepened further in lecture 542), or a sudden change in response length distribution that often signals a prompt or model-version regression. The core design tension in any alerting system is sensitivity versus alert fatigue: thresholds set too tight generate constant false alarms that teams learn to ignore (eventually missing a real incident buried in noise), while thresholds set too loose miss real problems; the practical fix is tiered severity (a "page someone now" tier for user-impacting issues versus a "review during business hours" tier for early-warning signals) and alerting on sustained trends over a time window rather than single noisy data points. An alerting system's real test is not how many conditions it watches, but whether the on-call engineer trusts every page enough to act on it immediately. |
| **Worked example**      | An ML service's alerting rules page an on-call engineer immediately if error rate exceeds 5% for more than 3 minutes (user-impacting, high confidence), but only creates a lower-priority ticket for review if the automated quality-evaluation score drifts down by 10% over a rolling 24-hour window (early warning, needs human judgment to confirm it's real before waking anyone up).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why is tiered alert severity important for an ML/LLM service's alerting design?

**(A) It prevents alert fatigue by reserving immediate pages for high-confidence, user-impacting issues while routing early-warning signals to lower-priority review**

\(B\) All alerts should always page someone immediately regardless of confidence or impact

\(C\) Tiering alerts has no effect on whether on-call engineers trust and act on pages

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design 3 alerting rules for a hypothetical ML/LLM service: one infrastructure alert, one quality/drift alert, and one cost alert, each with its severity tier and threshold.

**Lecture 541 SLOs and SLIs for AI services**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Advanced MLOps + Observability · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define service-level indicators and objectives appropriate for an AI service, including quality-based SLIs beyond latency and uptime.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | A service-level indicator (SLI) is a specific measured metric (e.g. p95 latency, error rate); a service-level objective (SLO) is a target for that metric over a time window (e.g. "p95 latency under 2 seconds for 99.5% of requests over a rolling 30 days"), and together they define what "working well enough" concretely means for a service, which then drives alerting thresholds and incident prioritization. AI services need SLIs beyond the standard latency/error-rate/uptime set used for typical web services: an answer-quality SLI (from automated evaluation sampling or user feedback signals), a groundedness or hallucination-rate SLI for a RAG system, and a cost-per-request SLI tying back to Month 31's cost-management content, since an AI service can be "up" and fast while silently producing unacceptable answers, which traditional SLOs would never catch. Setting realistic SLO targets requires baseline data -- measuring current performance for a few weeks before committing to a target -- and revisiting SLOs periodically, since a model upgrade or traffic pattern change can shift what's achievable; an SLO that was realistic at launch can silently become either too lax or impossible to hit six months later if nobody revisits it. |
| **Worked example**      | A RAG customer-support service sets an SLO of "groundedness score (as measured by an automated evaluator) above 0.85 for at least 98% of sampled responses over a rolling week," in addition to standard latency and uptime SLOs, specifically because a prior incident saw the service remain fully "up" and fast while quietly hallucinating incorrect policy details.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why do AI services need quality-based SLIs (like groundedness or hallucination rate) in addition to standard latency and uptime SLIs?

**(A) An AI service can be fully available and fast while still silently producing unacceptable or incorrect answers, which latency/uptime SLIs cannot detect**

\(B\) Quality-based SLIs are redundant once latency and uptime SLOs are defined

\(C\) AI services never need SLOs because their output quality is unmeasurable

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Define one quality-based SLI and a realistic SLO target for an AI service of your choice, explaining what baseline measurement you would take before committing to that target.

**Lecture 542 Advanced drift detection techniques**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Advanced MLOps + Observability · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply statistical tests for distribution shift (KS test, PSI, KL divergence) to detect data and prediction drift in production.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Building on Year 2 Month 24's introduction to drift monitoring, this lecture goes deeper into the actual statistical machinery: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test compares two samples' cumulative distributions and returns a p-value indicating whether they likely came from the same underlying distribution, well suited to a single continuous feature; Population Stability Index (PSI) buckets a feature into bins and measures how much the proportion of data in each bin has shifted between a baseline and current window, widely used in industry because it gives one interpretable number per feature with established rule-of-thumb thresholds (PSI above roughly 0.2 typically signals meaningful drift); and KL divergence measures how different two probability distributions are in an information-theoretic sense, useful for comparing prediction-output distributions or multi-class label distributions rather than just single continuous features. Choosing among these depends on the data type (continuous versus categorical) and whether you need a simple pass/fail signal (PSI) or a more statistically rigorous significance test (KS); importantly, none of these tests tells you why drift happened, so a drift alert from any of them should trigger human investigation into the underlying cause (a new user segment, a seasonal shift, an upstream data pipeline bug) before deciding whether retraining is actually the right response. |
| **Worked example**      | A fraud-detection model's input feature "average transaction amount" shows a PSI of 0.31 between this month's traffic and the training-period baseline, triggering a drift investigation that reveals a new high-value customer segment onboarded last month -- a legitimate population shift, not a data pipeline bug, informing the team's decision to retrain rather than investigate further for an error.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** What does a PSI value above the typical 0.2 threshold indicate, and what should an engineer do immediately after seeing it?

\(A\) It definitively proves the model is now broken and must be deleted immediately with no further investigation

**(B) It signals meaningful distribution shift in that feature, which should prompt human investigation into the cause before deciding on a response**

\(C\) It indicates a software bug in the monitoring system itself, not the data

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Using a dataset of your choice (synthetic or real), compute the PSI for one feature between two different time windows, and interpret whether the result signals meaningful drift.

**Lecture 543 Automated retraining pipelines with safety checks**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Advanced MLOps + Observability · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design an automated retraining pipeline that gates every promotion to production behind explicit safety checks.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | An automated retraining pipeline triggers when a condition is met (a scheduled interval, or a drift alert from lecture 542), pulls fresh labeled data, retrains the model, and then critically must pass through a series of safety checks before being promoted to serve real traffic: a held-out evaluation set comparison (the new model must meet or exceed the current production model's score on a fixed benchmark, not just perform well on the fresh training data it just saw), a fairness/bias check across key subgroups if applicable, a sanity check against known edge cases that have caused past incidents (a regression test set, directly analogous to Month 31's prompt-regression concept but for traditional ML retraining), and a human approval gate for high-stakes domains even when all automated checks pass. The entire point of these safety checks is that "the pipeline successfully produced a new model" and "the new model is actually better and safe to deploy" are two completely different claims, and conflating them -- auto-promoting any model the pipeline produces -- is how a subtly corrupted training batch or an unnoticed labeling error silently degrades a production system. |
| **Worked example**      | A retraining pipeline for a credit-risk model retrains weekly, but before any new model is promoted it must score at least as well as the current production model on a fixed golden evaluation set, pass a subgroup-fairness check across protected demographic categories, and pass regression tests against 15 historical edge cases that previously caused incidents -- with a human reviewer required to sign off even after all three automated checks pass, given the domain's regulatory stakes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why is it dangerous to automatically promote any model a retraining pipeline successfully produces?

**(A) Successfully retraining and actually being better/safe to deploy are different claims; a subtly bad training batch could produce a model that trains fine but performs worse or unsafely**

\(B\) Retraining pipelines never produce a materially different model so promotion gating is unnecessary busywork

\(C\) Automated safety checks are redundant once a model successfully finishes training

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design 3 specific safety checks you would require before auto-promoting a retrained model for a domain of your choice, and state what would happen if any one of them failed.

**Lecture 544 Canary and shadow deployment patterns for ML models, in depth**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Advanced MLOps + Observability · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
