|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply judgment built across the whole program to justify choosing a classical ML, deep learning, or LLM-based approach for a given problem's specific characteristics.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture synthesizes judgment built across the entire three-year program: classical ML (gradient boosted trees, logistic regression, covered in Year 1) remains the right default for structured/tabular data problems with moderate data volume, where it offers strong performance, fast training/inference, and genuine interpretability that a deep model usually can't match -- choosing a neural network here mainly adds complexity without a corresponding accuracy gain. Deep learning (covered through Year 2) is the right choice when the input is unstructured (images, audio, raw sequential signals) or when there's enough data and enough genuine signal in fine-grained patterns that a learned representation clearly outperforms hand-engineered features. An LLM-based approach (this program's Year 3 focus) fits best when the task involves open-ended natural language understanding or generation, when flexibility across many loosely related sub-tasks matters more than squeezing out maximum accuracy on one narrow task, or when the cost and latency of a large general-purpose model is acceptable given the task's value -- and importantly, defaulting to an LLM for every problem, including ones a simple classical model would solve more cheaply, accurately and interpretably, is a common and avoidable mistake that reveals a design candidate hasn't actually internalized this tradeoff. |
| **Worked example**      | For "predict whether a loan applicant will default" using structured financial fields, a gradient boosted tree is the right choice (interpretable, fast, strong on tabular data); for "summarize a customer's open-ended support conversation for a human agent," an LLM is the right choice given the unstructured, open-ended language understanding required -- using an LLM for the first problem or a boosted tree for the second would both be poor-fit choices.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why would defaulting to an LLM-based approach for a structured tabular-data prediction task typically be a poor design choice?

\(A\) LLMs are always the best choice for every type of prediction problem regardless of input structure

**(B) A classical ML model usually matches or exceeds an LLM's accuracy on structured tabular data while being faster, cheaper, and more interpretable**

\(C\) Classical ML models can never be used for prediction tasks of any kind

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For two different problems of your choosing (one structured/tabular, one open-ended language-based), justify in 2-3 sentences each which approach class (classical ML, deep learning, or LLM) fits best and why.

**Lecture 557 Designing the data pipeline for a large-scale AI system**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a data pipeline covering ingestion, labeling/feedback collection, storage, and feature computation for a large-scale AI system.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | A large-scale AI system's data pipeline must handle several distinct concerns together: ingestion (how raw events or documents enter the system, typically through a streaming queue for real-time data or batch jobs for periodic bulk data), labeling or feedback collection (how ground-truth signal gets attached to data -- explicit human labeling, or implicit feedback like clicks and conversions, each with different noise characteristics the downstream model and evaluation must account for), storage (a design decision between a data lake for raw/flexible storage and a structured warehouse or feature store for fast, consistent serving-time access, often using both for different purposes), and feature computation (built on Year 1-2's feature engineering content, now at scale, meaning point-in-time correctness becomes critical -- a feature computed using information that wouldn't have been available at serving time, called data leakage, silently invalidates a model's offline evaluation). The data pipeline is frequently the least glamorous but most failure-prone part of a large-scale AI system design, and a design that skips straight to the model while treating the data pipeline as an afterthought is a common and serious gap in an otherwise strong design. |
| **Worked example**      | A large-scale AI system's data pipeline ingests clickstream events via a streaming queue, computes a user-engagement feature in a feature store with careful point-in-time correctness (never using a click that happened after the prediction moment being trained on), and stores raw events separately in a data lake for future reprocessing if the feature definition changes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** What is data leakage in the context of a large-scale AI system's data pipeline, and why is it dangerous?

\(A\) It refers to a literal security breach of the data storage system

**(B) It occurs when a feature is computed using information that wouldn't have actually been available at serving time, silently inflating offline evaluation results**

\(C\) It refers to normal, expected redundancy between the data lake and feature store

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For an AI system design scenario, describe the ingestion method (streaming vs batch), the feedback signal type (explicit vs implicit), and one point-in-time correctness risk you'd specifically guard against in its feature pipeline.

**Lecture 558 Designing the serving/inference layer at scale**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a serving/inference layer for a large-scale AI system, choosing among synchronous, asynchronous, and precomputed serving patterns.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | The serving layer's design choice -- synchronous (compute the prediction live, on each request), asynchronous (queue the request and return the result later, suited to non-time-critical tasks), or precomputed (compute predictions ahead of time in a batch job and simply look them up at request time) -- depends directly on the latency budget and request pattern established during scale estimation (lecture 555): a recommendation feed for a small, relatively stable item catalog is often precomputable overnight, while a fraud-detection decision on a live transaction must be synchronous and fast. At large scale, the serving layer typically also needs a caching strategy (serving popular or recently computed predictions from a fast cache rather than recomputing), horizontal scaling behind a load balancer for the live inference path, and a clear decision about batching requests together for GPU efficiency (increases throughput and cost-efficiency but adds a small latency cost per request, directly trading off against the latency budget from estimation). A strong serving-layer design explicitly states why it chose synchronous versus async versus precomputed for this specific system, rather than defaulting to "call the model live" for every case, since a system serving stable predictions that could be precomputed overnight is wasting enormous compute re-deriving the same answer on every single request. |
| **Worked example**      | A video platform's "recommended for you" feed is precomputed in a nightly batch job per user and simply looked up at request time (since recommendations don't need to reflect the last few seconds of behavior), while its "is this payment fraudulent" decision is served synchronously with a tight latency budget, since that decision must be made before the transaction completes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why might precomputing predictions in a batch job be preferable to synchronous live inference for some AI system components?

\(A\) Precomputation is always strictly worse and should never be used for any component

**(B) When predictions don't need to reflect the most recent few seconds of data, precomputation avoids wastefully recomputing the same answer on every single request**

\(C\) Synchronous serving is impossible to implement at any scale

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For an AI system design scenario, identify one component that should be served synchronously and one that could be precomputed, justifying each choice based on its latency and freshness requirements.

**Lecture 559 Designing for consistency, caching and latency in a large AI system**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design caching and consistency strategies for a large-scale AI system, reasoning explicitly about staleness tolerance.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Caching at scale introduces a consistency tradeoff that must be reasoned about explicitly for each cached value: a strongly consistent design always reflects the latest underlying data but sacrifices the latency and cost benefit caching exists to provide, while an eventually consistent design (serving a cached value that may be slightly stale) accepts some staleness in exchange for much lower latency and cost -- and the right choice depends entirely on how much staleness the specific use case can tolerate, which varies hugely within one system (a user's account balance typically needs strong consistency; a "trending now" ranking can tolerate being a few minutes stale with no real harm). Cache invalidation strategy (time-based expiry versus event-driven invalidation when the underlying data changes) and cache key design (what exactly gets cached -- a full computed response, or an intermediate feature value reused across many requests) both need explicit design decisions rather than defaults, since an overly aggressive cache can serve stale, wrong predictions for far longer than intended, while an overly conservative cache provides little latency benefit at all. A mature design explicitly states the staleness tolerance for each cached component rather than treating "add a cache" as a single undifferentiated decision applied uniformly across the whole system. |
| **Worked example**      | In a recommendation system, the ranked list of "trending products" is cached with a 5-minute time-based expiry (acceptable staleness for a ranking that changes slowly), while the check for "is this specific item still in stock" is never cached and always queried live, since serving a stale out-of-stock item as available would directly harm the user experience.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** Why should caching decisions be made per-component rather than as one uniform policy across an entire system?

**(A) Different components have very different staleness tolerances, so a uniform caching policy either serves dangerously stale data somewhere or wastes the latency benefit elsewhere**

\(B\) Caching should never be used anywhere in a well-designed AI system

\(C\) All components in any system always have identical staleness tolerance

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For an AI system design scenario, identify two components with clearly different staleness tolerance, and specify a caching/invalidation strategy appropriate to each.

**Lecture 560 Trading off accuracy against latency/cost at the system level**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Reason explicitly about the three-way tradeoff between model accuracy, serving latency, and compute cost at a full-system level.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | At the system level, accuracy, latency and cost form a three-way tradeoff where improving one typically costs one of the other two: a larger, more accurate model generally costs more to serve and responds more slowly, while a smaller, faster, cheaper model sacrifices some accuracy -- and the correct point on this tradeoff surface is not a universal optimum but depends entirely on the business impact of each dimension for this specific system (a search ranking system might tolerate a small accuracy loss for a large latency win since users abandon slow searches, while a medical diagnosis-support system should weight accuracy far more heavily even at meaningfully higher latency and cost). A common and powerful technique for navigating this tradeoff at the system level, rather than the single-model level, is a cascade or tiered-model architecture: a fast, cheap, less accurate model handles the easy majority of cases, escalating only the harder or more ambiguous cases to a slower, more accurate (and more expensive) model, which often achieves a better overall accuracy/latency/cost balance than deploying one single model sized for the hardest cases across all traffic. Strong system-design answers name this specific tradeoff explicitly and justify where on it the given system should sit, rather than silently optimizing for one dimension (usually accuracy) while ignoring the other two. |
| **Worked example**      | A content-moderation system routes the large majority of clearly benign or clearly violating content through a fast, cheap classifier, escalating only the ambiguous middle cases to a slower, more accurate, more expensive model (or a human reviewer), achieving strong overall accuracy without paying the latency and cost of running the expensive model on every single piece of content.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main advantage of a tiered/cascade model architecture over deploying one single model sized for the hardest cases?

**(A) It usually achieves a better overall accuracy/latency/cost balance by reserving the expensive, accurate model only for genuinely hard or ambiguous cases**

\(B\) Cascade architectures are always strictly worse than a single uniform model

\(C\) Tiered architectures eliminate the need to ever consider latency or cost

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For an AI system design scenario, propose a two-tier cascade (a fast/cheap first stage and a slower/accurate escalation stage), stating what triggers escalation from the first tier to the second.

**Lecture 561 Designing for failure: graceful degradation when a model or dependency is unavailable**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design graceful-degradation behavior for an AI system's key components, building on Month 32's reliability content at the whole-system design level.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Designing for failure at the system-design level means explicitly specifying, for each major component, what the system does when that component is unavailable, rather than implicitly assuming every dependency is always up -- building directly on Month 32's reliability patterns but now applied during initial architecture design rather than retrofitted afterward. For a model-serving dependency, graceful degradation might mean falling back to a simpler rule-based heuristic or a cached previous prediction rather than failing the whole request; for a feature-store or data dependency, it might mean serving with a reduced feature set (slightly lower accuracy) rather than refusing to serve at all; and for a downstream action dependency (e.g. a payment system an agent would call), it might mean queuing the action for later retry rather than losing it. The system-design skill specifically being tested here is naming the single points of failure in a proposed architecture and, for each one, stating a concrete degraded-but-functional behavior rather than simply acknowledging "of course we'd add redundancy" without specifying what the degraded path actually does -- a vague gesture at reliability is a common tell that a design hasn't actually been thought through at this level of detail. |
| **Worked example**      | In a ride-sharing ETA-prediction system, if the real-time traffic-data dependency becomes unavailable, the system falls back to historical average travel times for that route and time of day rather than failing to show any ETA at all -- a specific, named degraded behavior rather than a vague "we'd handle that failure gracefully" statement.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** What distinguishes a strong system-design answer about failure handling from a weak one?

**(A) A strong answer names the specific single points of failure and states a concrete degraded-but-functional behavior for each, rather than vaguely gesturing at 'handling failures gracefully'**

\(B\) A strong answer asserts that failures will never occur in a well-designed system

\(C\) Failure handling is not a meaningful part of system design and can be omitted

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For an AI system design scenario, identify two single points of failure in your proposed architecture and state a specific degraded-but-functional behavior for each.

**Lecture 562 Presenting an AI system design to stakeholders/interviewers clearly**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Structure and deliver a clear verbal or written presentation of an AI system design to a non-technical-leaning or mixed audience.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Presenting a system design clearly means structuring the explanation top-down rather than bottom-up: start with the problem and the key requirements/constraints (so the audience has the same frame the designer used), then the high-level approach and the reasoning behind the major tradeoffs made (why this model class, why this serving pattern), and only then the detailed architecture -- reversing this order, starting with low-level implementation details before the audience understands what problem those details solve, is the single most common way a technically sound design presentation fails to land with its audience. Equally important is naming the tradeoffs explicitly rather than presenting the chosen design as the only possible correct answer: a strong presentation says "I chose X over Y because of this specific constraint, and here's what we give up by not choosing Y," which both demonstrates genuine understanding and invites useful pushback from stakeholders who may know a constraint the designer didn't have. For an interview setting specifically, narrating the reasoning process out loud as it unfolds (rather than presenting only a finished, polished answer) is usually more valuable to the interviewer than a flawless final architecture delivered with no visible reasoning, since the reasoning process is what's actually being evaluated. |
| **Worked example**      | A designer presenting a fraud-detection system design to a mixed audience of engineers and business stakeholders opens with the business cost of false positives versus false negatives (framing stakeholders care about), then the chosen cascade-model approach and why, and only then the specific feature pipeline details -- rather than opening with feature-engineering specifics before anyone in the room knows what business problem those features serve.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why does presenting the problem and requirements before the low-level architecture details improve a system design presentation?

**(A) It gives the audience the same frame the designer used, so the subsequent tradeoff reasoning and details actually make sense to them**

\(B\) Presentation order has no effect on whether an audience understands a design

\(C\) Low-level implementation details should always be presented first regardless of audience

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a 5-sentence outline for presenting one AI system design (problem/requirements, approach and key tradeoff, then one architecture detail) in the top-down order described.

**Lecture 563 Worked walkthrough of one complete AI system design end to end**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through one complete AI system design end to end, applying every step from lectures 554-562 in sequence to a concrete example.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture works a single example -- designing a large-scale fraud-detection system -- completely through the full process: requirements (minimize financial loss from fraud while keeping false-positive friction low for legitimate customers, decision must complete before a transaction is approved), scale estimate (millions of transactions per day, sub-200ms latency budget per decision), approach choice (a classical gradient-boosted model for the real-time first pass, given structured transaction features and the need for very fast, interpretable decisions, with a cascade escalating ambiguous cases to a slower deep model or human review), data pipeline (streaming transaction ingestion, a feature store computing account-history features with strict point-in-time correctness to avoid leakage), serving layer (synchronous, low-latency, heavily cached for account-level features that don't change every millisecond), failure design (if the real-time feature store is unavailable, fall back to a simpler rule-based check rather than blocking all transactions), and presentation (framed around the false-positive/false-negative business tradeoff first). Walking one example through every single step, rather than discussing the steps abstractly, is what turns lectures 554-562's individual concepts into one coherent, rehearsed reasoning process a learner can then apply to a genuinely new problem under real time pressure. |
| **Worked example**      | In this worked example, the decision to use a classical gradient-boosted model rather than an LLM for the primary fraud check follows directly from lecture 556's framework: the input is structured transaction data, the latency budget is extremely tight, and interpretability for compliance/audit purposes matters -- all pointing away from an LLM-based approach despite LLMs being the program's most recent major topic.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** In this worked fraud-detection example, why is a classical gradient-boosted model chosen over an LLM-based approach for the primary real-time check?

\(A\) LLMs are categorically incapable of ever being used in any fraud-related system

**(B) The structured input, extremely tight latency budget, and compliance need for interpretability all favor classical ML over an LLM, per the framework from lecture 556**

\(C\) Classical models are chosen here purely because they are older and more familiar

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick a different system (e.g. a content-recommendation system) and walk it through the same full sequence (requirements, scale, approach choice, data pipeline, serving, failure design, presentation framing) in your own words, one or two sentences per step.

**Lecture 564 Building the AI platform architecture project: part 1 (design document)**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Produce a complete design document for the month's AI platform architecture project, applying the full end-to-end process.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture begins the month's signature project: selecting one AI system design problem (either one provided or one of the learner's own choosing, at a meaningful scope -- not trivially simple) and producing a complete design document following the exact sequence from lectures 554-562: a scope statement with explicit assumptions, a scale estimate with reasoning shown, a justified approach-class choice, the data pipeline design, the serving-layer design, the caching/consistency strategy, the accuracy/latency/cost tradeoff reasoning, and the failure-handling design naming specific degraded behaviors for at least two single points of failure. This design document is deliberately produced in full before any presentation work begins in part 2, mirroring the discipline already rehearsed in Months 31 and 32's projects: a design written out completely and rigorously, independent of how it will later be presented, produces a stronger and more defensible final design than one shaped prematurely around how it will sound in a five-minute pitch. |
| **Worked example**      | A learner chooses "design a system to recommend relevant job postings to users" and produces a design document covering: scope (new users without history need a cold-start path; stated assumption that engagement, not just clicks, is the target metric), scale estimate (10 million users, estimated requests/second and latency budget), approach (a hybrid of classical collaborative filtering plus an LLM-based re-ranker for cold-start users using profile text), data pipeline, serving layer (largely precomputed with a live re-ranking step), and failure design (falling back to popularity-based recommendations if the personalization service is unavailable).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture require the full design document to be completed before any presentation work begins in part 2?

\(A\) Because presentation work and design work are identical and can be done simultaneously with no distinction

**(B) A design produced independent of how it will be presented tends to be more rigorous and defensible than one prematurely shaped around a short pitch**

\(C\) Because design documents are never actually needed in real system-design work

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Choose an AI system design problem and write your full design document following the lectures 554-562 sequence: scope/assumptions, scale estimate, approach justification, data pipeline, serving layer, caching strategy, accuracy/latency/cost tradeoff, and failure handling for at least two single points of failure.

**Lecture 565 Building and evaluating the AI platform architecture project: part 2 (presenting the design)**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Deliver a clear top-down presentation of the completed design document and evaluate it against the month's full criteria.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Part 2 takes the completed design document from part 1 and applies lecture 562's presentation principles: structuring a top-down walkthrough (problem/requirements first, then approach and key tradeoffs, then details), explicitly naming at least one major tradeoff and what was given up by not choosing the alternative, and practicing narrating the reasoning process rather than only presenting a polished final answer. Evaluation closes the project against concrete criteria drawn from the whole month: does the design document address every step from lectures 554-562 (not skipping scale estimation or failure design, two steps commonly skipped under time pressure), is the approach-class choice (lecture 556) actually justified by the problem's specific characteristics rather than just the program's most recently covered topic, and does the presentation genuinely lead with requirements and tradeoffs rather than diving straight into implementation details. This full design-then-present-then-evaluate cycle is the explicit rehearsal for a real system-design interview or a real stakeholder design review, which is this month's stated professional framing. |
| **Worked example**      | A learner presents their job-recommendation system design starting with the cold-start problem and the engagement-versus-click tradeoff (requirements first), then the hybrid collaborative-filtering-plus-LLM-reranker approach and why a pure LLM approach was rejected as too costly at this request volume (approach and tradeoff), then architecture details -- and in self-evaluation notes that their original design document under-specified the failure path for the re-ranking service, honestly flagging the gap.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** What two steps from the lectures 554-562 sequence are most commonly skipped under time pressure, and why does evaluation specifically check for them?

**(A) Scale estimation and failure design are commonly skipped, so evaluation checks for them because omitting either produces a design that looks complete but hasn't actually confronted real constraints**

\(B\) Every step is always included under time pressure with none more at risk than another

\(C\) Presentation structure and requirements-gathering are the two most commonly skipped steps

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Present your project design following the top-down structure (requirements, approach and key tradeoff, then details), then evaluate your own design document against the full lectures 554-562 checklist, honestly noting any step you under-specified.

**Lecture 566 Common failure patterns in AI system design reasoning**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI System Design · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Identify and avoid the most common reasoning failure patterns that weaken an otherwise technically sound AI system design.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Beyond the individual steps already covered, several recurring failure patterns weaken system design reasoning regardless of technical correctness: jumping to a specific technology or model name before establishing requirements (the single most common failure, already flagged in lecture 553); treating the design as a single monolithic decision rather than naming the specific tradeoffs at each layer (data pipeline, serving, failure handling) separately; defaulting to the most recently learned or most fashionable technique (an LLM, in this program's current context) without justifying it against the problem's actual characteristics per lecture 556's framework; and presenting a design with false confidence, never naming any weakness or alternative considered, which paradoxically reads as less credible than a design that explicitly acknowledges its tradeoffs and remaining open questions. Recognizing these patterns in one's own reasoning -- ideally by reviewing a completed design against this exact list before presenting it -- is a concrete, practiced way to catch avoidable weaknesses before a stakeholder or interviewer catches them first. |
