|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Systematically review every project built across the 3-year program and shortlist the 6-10 strongest as flagship candidates.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | With roughly 36 months of projects behind them, a student cannot showcase everything -- the professional move is a deliberate audit: list every project built since Month 1, score each on technical depth, polish, and how well it demonstrates a skill relevant to the student's target role, and shortlist only the 6-10 strongest as flagship projects, retiring or merging the rest into a single 'other work' mention rather than diluting the portfolio's impact with mediocre entries. |
| **Worked example**      | A student targeting ML engineering roles might shortlist the Month 16 production ML system, the Month 21 IBM AI Engineering capstone, the Month 30 responsible-AI project, and the Month 34 end-to-end AI product as flagships, while a solid but unremarkable Month 6 data-cleaning exercise is left out entirely.                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why should a 3-year portfolio showcase only 6-10 flagship projects rather than all projects ever built?

\(A\) A longer list of projects always impresses a reviewer more than a short, curated one

**(B) A curated set of the strongest projects demonstrates depth and quality clearly, while a long undifferentiated list dilutes impact and asks a time-constrained reviewer to do the curation themselves**

\(C\) GitHub technically limits an account to 10 repositories

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** List every project you've built across the 3-year program, score each on technical depth and polish, and shortlist your top 6-10 candidates for flagship status.

**Lecture 590 What makes a project portfolio-worthy**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Distinguish a genuinely portfolio-worthy project from a mere learning exercise, by the standard of README quality, reproducibility, tests, and a clear story.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | A learning exercise can be a rough notebook that technically works; a portfolio-worthy project needs a clear README explaining what problem it solves and why, genuine reproducibility (someone else can actually clone and run it), at least some tests demonstrating the code works as claimed, and a coherent narrative connecting the problem to the approach to the result -- a project missing any of these isn't ready for flagship status no matter how sophisticated its underlying technique. |
| **Worked example**      | A sophisticated transformer fine-tuning project with no README beyond a file list, uncommented code, and no way to reproduce the reported results is not portfolio-worthy regardless of how advanced the technique is, until those gaps are fixed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** What can disqualify a technically sophisticated project from flagship portfolio status?

\(A\) Nothing; technical sophistication alone always qualifies a project for flagship status

**(B) Missing a clear README, genuine reproducibility, basic tests, or a coherent narrative -- any of which can undermine a reviewer's ability to actually trust and understand the work**

\(C\) Using an older model architecture than the current state of the art

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick one project from your Lecture 589 shortlist and honestly audit it against these four criteria (README, reproducibility, tests, narrative), listing which are currently missing.

**Lecture 591 Writing a compelling top-level GitHub profile README**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Write the special README.md that appears at the top of a GitHub profile, introducing the student professionally in the first few seconds a recruiter sees it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | GitHub profile READMEs (created via a repository named exactly after the username) render at the top of a profile page and are often the very first thing a recruiter sees -- a strong one states, in the first two lines, who the student is and what they do, highlights 2-3 standout flagship projects with direct links, and lists core technical skills, all written for a 15-30 second skim rather than as a full autobiography. |
| **Worked example**      | Opening with 'AI/ML engineer specialising in applied generative AI and production ML systems -- see my RAG-based document assistant and production fraud-detection pipeline below' immediately orients a skimming recruiter, unlike an unstructured paragraph of personal history.                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why should a GitHub profile README be written for a 15-30 second skim rather than as a detailed autobiography?

\(A\) Recruiters always read every word of every profile they encounter in full detail

**(B) A recruiter screening many candidates typically skims quickly, so the most important information (who you are, your best work) must be immediately visible, not buried in lengthy prose**

\(C\) GitHub technically limits profile README length to a few words

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write your own GitHub profile README: a 2-line professional identity statement, links to your 2-3 standout flagship projects, and a core skills list.

**Lecture 592 Organizing a GitHub profile for a recruiter's skim**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Configure pinned repositories, consistent naming, and clear descriptions so a GitHub profile reads coherently at a glance.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | Beyond the profile README, GitHub lets a user pin up to 6 repositories to the top of their profile -- pin exactly the flagship projects from Lecture 589, give each a consistent, professional naming convention (not \`project1\`, \`final-v2-actually-final\`), and write a one-line repository description (GitHub's own description field, visible in the pinned-repo grid) that states what the project does in plain language before a reviewer even opens it. |
| **Worked example**      | A profile with 6 pinned repositories named \`rag-document-assistant\`, \`fraud-detection-pipeline\`, and similarly clear names, each with a one-line description like 'Production-style fraud detection pipeline with monitoring and drift detection,' reads immediately coherently, unlike a profile pinning \`hw3\` or \`test-repo\`.                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** What should a GitHub repository's one-line description field accomplish for a portfolio project?

\(A\) Nothing; the description field is rarely seen and doesn't matter

**(B) State clearly, in plain language, what the project does, so a reviewer understands its purpose before even opening the repository**

\(C\) List every library and dependency used in the project

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pin your 6-10 flagship repositories (or your closest equivalent), rename any unclear ones, and write a one-line description for each.

**Lecture 593 Polishing each flagship project's README**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Bring each flagship project's own README to a professional standard matching Lecture 590's portfolio-worthy criteria.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | Beyond the top-level profile README, each individual flagship repository needs its own professional README: a clear project title and one-sentence summary, the problem being solved and why it matters, the approach taken, key results or a demo (a screenshot, a sample output, or a metric), setup/reproduction instructions, and an honest note on limitations -- the single document determining whether a reviewer who clicks into this specific repository understands and trusts the work. |
| **Worked example**      | A flagship README with a results section reporting '92% F1 on held-out test data, see \`eval_results.json\` for the full breakdown' alongside a one-paragraph honest limitations note is far more credible to a technical reviewer than a README offering only a feature list.                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why should a flagship project's README include an honest limitations section rather than only listing strengths?

\(A\) Limitations sections make a project look weaker and should always be omitted from a portfolio

**(B) Acknowledging real limitations signals mature, honest engineering judgment to a technical reviewer, which builds more credibility than an unqualified list of strengths alone**

\(C\) Limitations are only relevant for academic papers, never for a portfolio project

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Rewrite one flagship project's README to include all the elements listed in this lecture: summary, problem/approach, results or demo, setup instructions, and an honest limitations note.

**Lecture 594 Writing a project case study: framing impact and metrics**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Write a short case-study framing for a flagship project that foregrounds its real-world impact and measurable results, distinct from its technical README.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | A README explains how a project works; a case study explains why it matters -- in 3-4 short paragraphs, state the problem in terms a non-technical reader would recognise, the approach taken (briefly, without deep technical jargon), the measurable outcome (an accuracy number, a latency improvement, a cost reduction, or a realistic estimate of one), and what the student learned or would do differently -- this is the piece most directly reusable in a resume bullet or interview answer. |
| **Worked example**      | A case study stating 'Reduced manual document-review time by an estimated 70% by building an AI assistant that surfaces the 3 most relevant passages for a given question, evaluated against 50 real analyst queries' gives a concrete, quotable impact statement a technical README alone would not surface as clearly.                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** How does a project case study differ in purpose from the project's own technical README?

\(A\) They serve the identical purpose and audience, so writing both is redundant

**(B) A case study foregrounds real-world impact and measurable outcomes for a broader audience, while the README explains technical implementation details for someone who wants to run or extend the code**

\(C\) A case study replaces the need for any technical documentation at all

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a 3-4 paragraph case study for one flagship project, including a measurable (or realistically estimated) outcome statement.

**Lecture 595 Adding tests and CI badges to flagship projects**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Add automated tests and a visible CI status badge to a flagship project to signal engineering rigor beyond working code alone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Building on Year 2 Month 23's CI/CD content, add at least a handful of real automated tests (covering key functions or the critical path of the pipeline) to a flagship project, wire up a CI workflow that runs them automatically on every push, and display the resulting pass/fail badge prominently at the top of the README -- a small addition that visibly signals to a technical reviewer that the project is maintained with real engineering discipline, not just demo code. |
| **Worked example**      | A README showing a green 'build passing' badge at the top, backed by a CI workflow that actually runs 8 real unit tests on every push, tells a technical reviewer in one glance that this project is held to a real engineering standard.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** What does a visible CI status badge communicate to a technical reviewer beyond the badge's literal pass/fail state?

\(A\) Nothing beyond the literal current test result shown

**(B) That the project has real automated tests wired into an active CI pipeline, signalling ongoing engineering discipline rather than one-off demo code**

\(C\) That the project uses a specific programming language

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Add at least 5 real automated tests to one flagship project, set up a CI workflow to run them automatically, and add the resulting status badge to that project's README.

**Lecture 596 Building a unified portfolio presentation layer**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a portfolio website or structured document that presents all flagship projects together under one consistent narrative.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | Individual project READMEs work for a reviewer who clicks into GitHub, but a unified presentation layer -- a simple portfolio website or a single well-formatted document -- gives a reviewer one place to see all 6-10 flagship projects together, framed by a consistent personal narrative (the student's specific focus area and what connects the projects), rather than requiring them to piece that story together themselves across separate repositories. |
| **Worked example**      | A simple portfolio site with one paragraph framing 'I build production-grade generative AI systems with a strong focus on evaluation and observability,' followed by 6 project cards each linking to its GitHub repo and case study, lets a reviewer grasp the student's overall positioning in under a minute.                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a unified portfolio presentation layer valuable in addition to well-polished individual GitHub repositories?

\(A\) GitHub repositories alone always communicate a candidate's overall positioning just as effectively

**(B) It presents all flagship projects together under one consistent narrative, saving a reviewer from having to infer the connecting story themselves by visiting each repository separately**

\(C\) A unified presentation layer is only useful for non-technical roles

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Build a simple portfolio website or single structured document presenting all your flagship projects with one consistent framing paragraph and a card or section per project.

**Lecture 597 Crafting a resume reflecting the 3-year program**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Write a resume that accurately reflects the skills developed across the 3-year program and highlights the flagship portfolio.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | A resume for this program's graduate should state the specific technical skill progression honestly (classical ML, deep learning, generative AI/RAG/agents, MLOps, cloud AI, system design) without inflating any single month's exposure into false seniority, link directly to the portfolio and 2-3 flagship projects with one quantified outcome line each (reusing Lecture 594's case-study metrics), and list earned certifications by their exact official names -- credibility here depends on precise, verifiable claims, not impressive-sounding but vague ones. |
| **Worked example**      | A resume bullet reading 'Built a production-style RAG document assistant reducing estimated manual review time by 70%, with full observability and CI testing (see portfolio link)' is precise and verifiable; 'Expert in all areas of artificial intelligence' is vague and immediately suspect to any technical reviewer.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why does resume credibility depend on precise, verifiable claims rather than broad, impressive-sounding ones?

\(A\) Broad claims are always more persuasive to a technical hiring manager than specific ones

**(B) A precise, verifiable claim (with a measurable outcome and a link to the actual work) can be checked and trusted, while vague claims invite skepticism from any reviewer with real technical experience**

\(C\) Resumes are never actually checked against the underlying portfolio work

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write or revise your resume's skills and project sections to use precise, verifiable claims with quantified outcomes and direct portfolio links, following this lecture's standard.

**Lecture 598 Tailoring portfolio presentation for different target roles**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Adjust which flagship projects and framing are emphasised depending on whether the target role is ML engineer, AI engineer, or applied scientist.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | The same 6-10 flagship projects can be framed differently depending on the target role: an ML engineer-focused presentation emphasises production systems, deployment, and MLOps rigor (Month 16, 23, 32 work); an AI engineer-focused presentation emphasises LLM applications, RAG, and agent systems (Month 25-29 work); an applied scientist-focused presentation emphasises rigorous evaluation methodology and experimentation (Month 9-10, 33 work) -- the portfolio's underlying projects stay the same, but which ones lead and how they're described shifts to match what each role actually values. |
| **Worked example**      | For an ML engineer application, leading with the Month 16 production ML pipeline and its monitoring setup makes sense; for an AI engineer application to the same company, leading instead with the Month 27 agent-based product and its tool-use design would resonate more with that specific hiring team.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why would a student present the same underlying portfolio differently depending on the target role, rather than using one fixed presentation for every application?

\(A\) Different roles require building an entirely separate set of projects from scratch

**(B) Different roles value different aspects of the same work, so leading with the project and framing most relevant to a specific role's priorities makes the strongest impression for that application**

\(C\) Tailoring the presentation would be dishonest regardless of the role being targeted

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write two short (3-4 sentence) portfolio framing intros for the same flagship project set: one tailored for an ML engineer role, one for an AI engineer role, highlighting what changes.

**Lecture 599 Preparing to discuss a flagship project in a technical interview**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Anticipate and prepare answers for the design-decision and tradeoff questions a flagship project is likely to draw in a technical interview.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | A flagship project listed on a resume will be interrogated in an interview, not just read -- prepare by listing the 3-5 most significant design decisions made in the project (why this model over an alternative, why this architecture, what tradeoff was accepted), writing a clear, honest answer for each including what would be done differently with more time, and practising explaining the project's story (problem, approach, result) out loud in under 2 minutes before diving into any one detail. |
| **Worked example**      | Being able to answer 'why did you choose a vector database over a simple keyword search for retrieval here?' with a clear, specific tradeoff explanation (recall on semantically-similar-but-differently-worded queries, at the cost of some latency and infrastructure complexity) demonstrates far more real understanding than a vague 'it seemed like the right choice.'                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why must a candidate prepare specific answers to anticipated design-decision questions rather than relying on familiarity with the project alone?

\(A\) Interviewers never ask about specific design decisions behind a listed project

**(B) Being able to clearly articulate a specific tradeoff reasoning demonstrates genuine understanding, which a vague or unprepared answer fails to convey even if the candidate built the project competently**

\(C\) Memorised code details are always more important than design reasoning in a technical interview

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For one flagship project, list its 3-5 most significant design decisions and write a clear, honest spoken-style answer for each, including what you'd do differently with more time.

**Lecture 600 LinkedIn and professional online presence**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Set up a LinkedIn profile and basic professional online presence consistent with and linking to the GitHub portfolio.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | A technical portfolio's reach is limited if it's only discoverable via a direct GitHub link -- a consistent LinkedIn profile (matching the resume's framing from Lecture 597, linking to the portfolio site, listing earned certifications) extends discoverability to recruiters who search there first, and consistency across GitHub, the portfolio site, and LinkedIn (same framing, same flagship projects highlighted) avoids presenting a confusing, fragmented professional identity across platforms. |
| **Worked example**      | A LinkedIn headline reading 'AI/ML Engineer \| Generative AI & Production ML Systems \| \[portfolio link\]' that matches the GitHub profile README's framing exactly, rather than a generic 'Student' headline with no portfolio link, gives a recruiter a consistent, discoverable professional identity across both platforms.                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why does consistency between a GitHub profile and a LinkedIn profile matter for a job-seeking portfolio?

\(A\) Consistency across platforms has no effect on how a candidate is perceived

**(B) Inconsistent framing or missing links across platforms creates a confusing, fragmented impression, while consistency reinforces one clear professional identity wherever a recruiter encounters it**

\(C\) LinkedIn and GitHub serve completely unrelated purposes with no overlap in audience

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Update (or create) your LinkedIn profile with a headline and summary consistent with your resume framing, a link to your portfolio, and your earned certifications listed.

**Lecture 601 Getting external feedback on a portfolio**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Collect structured feedback on the finished portfolio from an outside reviewer and iterate on at least one substantive gap it reveals.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Mirroring Year 1 Month 12's peer-review discipline at full portfolio scale, ask someone outside the project (a peer, a mentor, or anyone with hiring-adjacent experience if available) to spend the realistic 30-60 seconds a recruiter would spend skimming the GitHub profile and portfolio site, then report what they understood, what confused them, and what stood out -- an outside reviewer unfamiliar with the work's internal context reliably surfaces framing or clarity gaps the builder has become blind to. |
| **Worked example**      | A reviewer who, after a genuine 30-second skim, cannot tell which of the 6 pinned projects is the strongest one has surfaced a real prioritisation gap in the profile's framing, exactly the kind of issue worth fixing before real job applications begin.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why is external feedback on a portfolio especially valuable compared to the student's own review of it?

\(A\) A portfolio's own builder always evaluates its clarity to an outside viewer at least as accurately as an actual outside viewer would

**(B) An outside reviewer isn't anchored to the builder's internal context, so they reliably notice confusing framing or unclear prioritisation the builder has stopped being able to see**

\(C\) External feedback on a portfolio has no realistic analogue to how an actual recruiter would review it

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Have at least one outside reviewer give you a timed, realistic skim-review of your portfolio, and make at least one concrete change to your profile or portfolio site based on what they reported.

**Lecture 602 Final portfolio project, part 1**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Select and polish the 6-10 flagship projects that will constitute the finished portfolio's substance.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Begin this month's capstone build: finalise the shortlist from Lecture 589, bring each selected project's README to the Lecture 593 standard, add a case study per Lecture 594 for at least the top 3, and add tests and a CI badge per Lecture 595 to at least one -- by the end of this stage, every flagship project individually meets a professional bar, even before the unifying presentation layer is built. |
| **Worked example**      | By this stage's end, clicking into any one of the 6-10 flagship repositories should show a reviewer a clear README, evidence of testing where added, and (for the top projects) a case study -- each project standing on its own as credible, professional work.                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** What is the concrete milestone this first project stage should reach?

\(A\) A finished portfolio website with all projects linked together

**(B) Every selected flagship project individually meeting a professional README/testing/case-study standard on its own, before any unifying presentation layer is built**

\(C\) A LinkedIn profile update

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Finalise your flagship project shortlist and bring each one's README (and, for your top 3, a case study) up to this month's professional standard.

**Lecture 603 Final portfolio project, part 2**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build the unifying presentation layer tying the polished flagship projects into one coherent, hireable portfolio.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Finish this month's capstone build: build the unified portfolio website or structured document (Lecture 596) presenting all polished flagship projects under one consistent narrative, update the GitHub profile README and pinned repositories (Lectures 591-592) to point to it, align the resume (Lecture 597) and LinkedIn profile (Lecture 600) with the same framing, and incorporate at least one change from external feedback (Lecture 601) -- the deliverable is a complete, internally consistent professional presence across all four surfaces: GitHub, portfolio site, resume, and LinkedIn. |
| **Worked example**      | A finished submission where the GitHub profile, portfolio site, resume, and LinkedIn profile all tell the same consistent story about the student's focus area and point to the same flagship projects represents a genuinely complete, hireable professional presence, not just a collection of separately polished pieces.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** What makes this stage's deliverable complete, beyond each individual piece (GitHub, portfolio site, resume, LinkedIn) being well-made on its own?

\(A\) Nothing further; each piece being individually well-made is already sufficient

**(B) The deliverable is complete only when all four surfaces are internally consistent with each other and incorporate real external feedback, not just each being separately polished**

\(C\) Only the portfolio website itself matters; the other three surfaces are optional extras

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Build your unified portfolio presentation layer, align your GitHub profile, resume, and LinkedIn with its framing, and confirm you've incorporated at least one change from Lecture 601's external feedback.

**Lecture 604 Month 35 Examination: GitHub + Portfolio Engineering**

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

| **Teacher explanation** | A 1-hour exam covering Lectures 589-603: auditing and selecting flagship projects, professional README and case-study writing, CI/testing signals, unified portfolio presentation, resume and role-tailored framing, interview preparation, LinkedIn presence, and external feedback, including a written portfolio-critique task. |
| **Worked example**      | A typical exam item: "Given a short description of a GitHub profile and resume, identify 2 specific gaps against this month's portfolio-worthiness standard and propose a concrete fix for each."                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** What does a typical exam item like this require, beyond recalling this month's checklist of topics?

\(A\) Only the ability to list this month's lecture titles from memory

**(B) Applying this month's professional-portfolio standards critically to a new, previously unseen example**

\(C\) Only knowledge of Git commands, unrelated to portfolio presentation judgment

**Month 36 Final Professional AI/ML Capstone**

*Allocation: 20 hours \| 20 lectures \| Level: Professional / Job-ready \| Project: Final Professional AI/ML Capstone Project*

**Lecture 605 Final capstone: project scoping**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional AI/ML Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Scope an original, professional-grade final capstone system drawing on any combination of the full 3-year curriculum.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | This is the program's last and largest project: choose an original AI/ML system -- not a repeat of the Month 34 product or an earlier assignment -- that genuinely draws on whatever combination of classical ML, deep learning, generative AI, RAG, agents, MLOps, cloud AI, or system design best fits a real problem the student cares about, and write a precise scope statement following Year-1 Month 12's discipline (exact question, data, and success criteria) but now at full professional scale, with no month-specific constraint limiting which techniques are in play. |
| **Worked example**      | A final capstone scoped as 'an agent-based research assistant that retrieves and synthesises findings across a user's own document library, evaluated on retrieval precision and synthesis accuracy against 20 hand-labelled queries' draws deliberately on RAG, agent, and evaluation skills from across multiple prior years, rather than being confined to a single month's technique.                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the final capstone deliberately allow drawing on any combination of techniques from the full 3-year curriculum, rather than being scoped to one specific month's material?

\(A\) Restricting the capstone to one month's technique would better demonstrate mastery

**(B) The final capstone is meant to demonstrate genuine, integrated professional judgment across the whole program, which requires freedom to combine whichever techniques a real problem actually calls for**

\(C\) Combining multiple techniques in one project is never done in real professional AI work

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a precise scope statement for your original final capstone project, explicitly naming which combination of techniques from across the 3-year program it will draw on and why.

**Lecture 606 Final capstone: requirements and system design**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional AI/ML Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply Month 33's full system-design process to the student's own chosen capstone project.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | Reapply Month 33's requirements-gathering and system-design process directly to this capstone: write down the functional and non-functional requirements (what it must do, and the latency/cost/scale constraints it must respect), diagram the end-to-end architecture, and identify the single highest-risk design decision in the system before building begins -- this is the same discipline Month 34 applied to a product, now applied to whichever system the student has personally chosen. |
| **Worked example**      | Identifying that a planned capstone's highest-risk design decision is whether to use a single large model call or a multi-step agent pipeline for its core task -- and writing down the latency/cost tradeoff behind that choice -- is exactly the kind of upfront design decision Month 33 trained students to make explicit rather than leave implicit.                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why repeat Month 33's full requirements-and-design process specifically for the capstone, rather than moving straight to building?

\(A\) Requirements and design documentation are only useful for a grader, not for the actual project

**(B) Making requirements and the architecture's highest-risk decision explicit before building catches a flawed design on paper, which is far cheaper to fix than discovering it mid-build**

\(C\) System design only matters for projects targeting production deployment

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write your capstone's functional and non-functional requirements, diagram its end-to-end architecture, and identify its single highest-risk design decision.

**Lecture 607 Final capstone: data and model work**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional AI/ML Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Source, prepare, and build or select the data and modelling components the capstone's chosen approach requires.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Depending on the capstone's scope, this stage means sourcing and cleaning a dataset and training/validating a model (if a classical ML or deep learning approach was chosen), or building and testing a retrieval pipeline over a real document set (if RAG was chosen), or defining and testing a set of tools for an agent (if an agent approach was chosen) -- in every case, applying full prior rigor: proper train/validation/test discipline for a trained model, or a held-out evaluation set of realistic queries for a RAG or agent system. |
| **Worked example**      | A capstone's RAG component should be evaluated against a held-out set of realistic queries never used while building the retrieval pipeline, exactly mirroring the train/test separation discipline used for a trained classical ML model, even though no model is being trained here.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why does even a non-model-training capstone component (like a RAG pipeline) still need a held-out evaluation set the component was never built or tuned against?

\(A\) Held-out evaluation only matters when a model is literally being trained with gradient descent

**(B) Evaluating only against examples already seen during building risks an overly optimistic, unreliable measure of how the component will actually perform on new, unseen input**

\(C\) RAG pipelines cannot be meaningfully evaluated at all

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Build and evaluate your capstone's core data/model/retrieval/tool component against a held-out set of test cases it was not built or tuned against, and report the result honestly.

**Lecture 609 Final capstone: scaling and cost considerations**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional AI/ML Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Reason concretely about how the capstone system's design would need to change to handle significantly more load or a tighter budget.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Beyond getting the system working at small scale, apply professional judgment about scaling: estimate roughly what would happen to latency and cost if usage grew by 10x or 100x, identify the component that would break or become unacceptably expensive first (the classic bottleneck), and describe at least one concrete architectural change (caching, batching, a cheaper model tier for simple cases, asynchronous processing) that would address it -- this reasoning is itself evidence of professional system-design maturity, even if the capstone is never actually deployed at that scale. |
| **Worked example**      | Recognising that a capstone calling a large LLM on every single request would become the dominant cost driver at 100x usage, and proposing a cheaper classifier to route simple requests away from the expensive model call, demonstrates exactly the kind of cost-aware architectural reasoning professional AI engineering requires.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why is reasoning about 10x or 100x scale valuable even for a capstone that will never actually run at that scale?

\(A\) Scale reasoning has no practical value unless the system is actually deployed at that scale

**(B) Identifying the bottleneck and a concrete mitigation demonstrates real professional system-design judgment about cost and scaling tradeoffs, which is itself a skill being assessed**

\(C\) Every AI system scales identically regardless of its specific architecture

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Estimate what would break or become too expensive in your capstone system at 10x and 100x usage, and describe one concrete architectural change that would address the bottleneck you identified.

**Lecture 610 Final capstone: observability and production-readiness**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional AI/ML Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

| **Teacher explanation** | Instrument the capstone with the same rigor Month 32 and Month 34 required of any real system: log key request metadata and relevant performance metrics, build a basic dashboard or summary view, and run a production-readiness check covering error handling, timeout behaviour, and what happens when a dependency (a model API, a database) is temporarily unavailable -- a capstone that works perfectly only when every dependency behaves ideally has not actually demonstrated production-readiness. |
| **Worked example**      | Deliberately simulating a failed call to an external model API and confirming the capstone system returns a clear error rather than crashing or hanging indefinitely is exactly the kind of production-readiness check this lecture requires, not just an assumption that dependencies will always succeed.                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why must a capstone be tested against a deliberately simulated dependency failure, not just against the normal happy path?

\(A\) Dependencies in a real system never actually fail, so this testing has no practical value

**(B) Real systems do encounter dependency failures, and a system with no tested behaviour for that case may crash or hang in exactly the situation where robustness matters most**

\(C\) Simulating failures is only relevant for systems that will be deployed publicly

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Instrument your capstone with logging and a basic metrics view, then deliberately simulate one dependency failure and confirm the system handles it without crashing or hanging.

**Lecture 611 Final capstone: safety and responsible-AI review**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional AI/ML Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

| **Teacher explanation** | Run the capstone through Month 30's full safety review: identify realistic misuse or abuse scenarios specific to this system (not generic ones), check for any fairness or bias concern relevant to its specific data or task, confirm the system's outputs are presented with appropriate honesty about uncertainty (Month 34's UX-for-limitations standard), and document any known, unmitigated risk openly rather than silently -- a capstone is not complete until this review has actually happened, regardless of how well its core technique performs. |
| **Worked example**      | A capstone recommendation system reviewed for whether its recommendations could systematically disadvantage a particular user subgroup, with that specific check documented in the final report (whether or not an issue was found), demonstrates the review genuinely happened rather than being skipped.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a safety and responsible-AI review need to be documented even when no serious issue is found?

\(A\) Documentation is unnecessary if the review happened to find nothing serious

**(B) Documenting that the review actually happened, and what was specifically checked, is itself evidence of due diligence, distinct from simply asserting the system is safe with no supporting detail**

\(C\) Safety reviews are only required for consumer-facing production systems, never for capstone projects

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Run a documented safety and responsible-AI review of your capstone covering misuse scenarios, fairness/bias concerns relevant to your specific task, and output-honesty, writing down what was checked and found.

| **Worked example**      | A test suite that includes a specific test asserting the system returns a clear error (not a crash) when given empty input, directly covering an edge case identified during the safety review, ties this lecture's testing work concretely back to Lecture 611's findings rather than testing generically.                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why should at least one test in the capstone's suite directly cover a specific edge case or misuse scenario identified during the safety review?

\(A\) Tests should only ever cover the system's happy-path behaviour

**(B) It provides concrete, automated evidence that a previously identified risk was actually mitigated, rather than just assumed to be handled**

\(C\) Edge-case testing is unrelated to a project's overall quality bar

**Lecture 620 Extra practice: system-design-review drill**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional AI/ML Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

| **Teacher explanation** | Additional depth lecture (replaces this month's original duplicated content): revisit the capstone's architecture from Lecture 606 with fresh eyes after the system has actually been built (Lectures 607-613), checking whether the as-built system still matches the original design, where it diverged and why, and whether a different design choice now looks better in hindsight -- real systems always drift from their initial design, and reviewing that drift explicitly is itself a professional system-design skill distinct from the upfront design pass alone. |
| **Worked example**      | Discovering that the capstone ended up using synchronous processing for a step originally planned as asynchronous, because the actual latency turned out lower than expected, is exactly the kind of honest as-built-versus-planned comparison this drill is meant to surface.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why is reviewing how a system's as-built architecture diverged from its original design a valuable skill distinct from the original upfront design pass?

\(A\) A system's final architecture always matches its original design exactly, so there is nothing to compare

**(B) Real systems commonly drift from their initial plan during building, and honestly reviewing that drift (and why it happened) is itself a distinct, valuable professional skill from the upfront design alone**

\(C\) Only the original design matters; the as-built system's actual architecture is irrelevant once it works

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Compare your capstone's original Lecture 606 architecture diagram to how the system actually ended up being built, and write 2-3 sentences on where it diverged and why.
